मतिान करने की अनुमजत िी िाएगी । ऐसी ििा में भुगतान की गई आपजत्त फीस िब् त कर ली िाएगी । (10) मतिान के अंत में ररटर्नंग अजधकारी एकजत्रत आपजत्त फीस, आपजत्त करने वाले ्‍ यजियों को वापस की गई फीस और िब् त की गई फीस का जहसाब तैयार करेगा और साथ में प्रत् येक मामले में संजिप् त िांच के पश् चातम उसके द्वारा जलए गए जनणायों का संजिप् त सार सोसाइटी को िेगा । (11) यदि मतिान के दकसी चरण में, िंगा या हंगामा द्वारा कायावाही अवरुद्ध या बाजधत होती है या यदि ऐसे जनवााचन में दकसी पयााप् त कारणों से मतिान कराना संभव नहीं है तो ररटर्नंग अजधकारी को मतिान रे करने के ऐसे कारणों को अजभलेजखत करने के पश् चातम, मतिान रे करने की िजि होगी । (12) मतिान के जलए जनयत समय के पश् चातम दकसी मतिाता को मतिान करने की अनुमजत नहीं िी िाएगी । परंतु दक यदि कोई मतिाता, मतिान के समय की समाजप्त के पूवा पररसर में प्रवेि कर चुका हो तो उसे मतपत्र िारी कर मतिान करने की अनुमजत िी िाएगी । (13) मतिान की समाजप्त के ीक पश् चातम मतगणना आरंभ की िाएगी और यदि ररटर्नंग अजधकारी के जनयंत्रण से परे यदि मतों की गणना तुरंत संभव नहीं है तो मतपेटी को ररटर्नंग अजधकारी और जनवााचन में खड़े अभ् यर्थायों या उनके एिेंटों के मुहरों से मुहरबंि कर दिया िाएगा, और यदि यह उनकी इच् छा हो तो मतपेरटयां सोसाइटी की सुरजित अजभरिा में िमा कर िी िाएगी और ऐसी जस्ट्थजत में ररटर्नंग अजधकारी अगले दिन आरंभ होने वाली मतगणना का स्ट् थान और समय की घोिणा करेगा और अभ् यथी और उसके अजभकतााओं को जलजखत में भी सूजचत करेगा और मतगणना अगले दिन ररटर्नंग अजधकारी द्वारा या उसके पयावेिण में की िाएगी और प्रत् येक अभ् यथी और उनके प्राजधकृत अजभकताा को मतगणना के समय उपजस्ट्थत रहने का अजधकार होगा तथा दकसी अभ् यथी या उसके अजभकताा के मतगणना में अनुपजस्ट्थत रहने से ररटर्नंग अजधकारी द्वारा मतगणना या पररणाम की घोिणा जनष् प्रभावी नहीं होगी । (14) ररटर्नंग अजधकारी द्वारा मतगणना की समाजप्त के पश् चातम, वह मतिान के पररणाम की एक जववरणी तैयार करेगा और प्राजधकरण के पूवाानुमोिन से तुरंत पररणाम घोजित करेगा ।

Primary Agricultural Credit Societies (PACS) are village- or panchayat-level cooperative societies that form the lowest tier of the Short-Term Cooperative Credit Structure. PACS deal directly with rural and agricultural borrowers. They provide loans, collect repayment of loans, and may undertake distribution and marketing functions. PACS are an important link between farmers and the higher levels of the cooperative credit system, including District Central Cooperative Banks (DCCBs), State Cooperative Banks (StCBs), and NABARD. --- ## Why are PACS Important? PACS help connect farmers and rural communities with: * Agricultural credit * Farm inputs * Agricultural services * Storage facilities * Markets and distribution * Other cooperative and government-supported services The Ministry of Cooperation describes PACS as the grassroots base of the cooperative credit structure. PACS can help bring farmers closer to credit, agricultural inputs, markets and value addition. --- ## What Services Can PACS Provide? Traditional PACS activities include: * Short-term agricultural credit * Medium-term credit * Distribution of seeds * Distribution of fertilizers * Distribution of pesticides * Storage-related services * Agricultural input services * Marketing and distribution functions * Loan repayment and related credit services Under the Model Bye-laws and diversification initiatives, PACS can also undertake multiple activities beyond traditional credit. These may include: * Dairy activities * Fisheries activities * Floriculture * Food-grain procurement * Warehousing and storage * Fair Price Shops * LPG/CNG/Petrol/Diesel distributorship * Common Service Centre (CSC) services * Business Correspondent or banking-related activities * Insurance-related services * Custom Hiring Centres * Other permitted business activities The exact activities available at an individual PACS depend on its applicable State Cooperative Societies Act, bye-laws, permissions and local implementation. --- ## What Types of Loans Does PACS Provide? PACS traditionally provide: * Short-term agricultural credit * Medium-term agricultural credit The Model Bye-laws and computerization framework also cover financial services involving short-, medium- and long-term loans. However, the exact loan products, limits, interest rates, repayment periods and eligibility conditions depend on the applicable cooperative rules, State provisions and the individual PACS or financing structure. 36 National Cooperative Database 2023 : A Report P rimary Agriculture Credit Societies (PACS) constitute the lowest tier of the Short-Term Cooperative Credit Structure (STCCS) in the country, primarily providing short-term and medium-term credit facility and other input services, like seed, fertilizer, pesticide distribution, etc. to member farmers. PACS are refinanced by NABARD through District Central Cooperative Banks (DCCBs) and State Cooperative Banks (StCBs). Being the grassroots level cooperative institutions, PACS play a crucial role in sustaining the rural economy of the country by purveying institutional credit to small and marginal farmers. PACS are governed by the Cooperative Acts of their respective states and guided by State Bye-laws. They engage directly with rural (agricultural) borrowers, extending loans, overseeing loan repayments, and managing marketing and distribution functions. Notably, the National Cooperative Database (NCD) portal records the presence of 1,03,304 PACS in the country, with around 95% (i.e., 98,486) of them are being functional in rural areas. Significantly, the growth of PACS has been substantial, expanding from approximately 2,982 PACS in 1900-1923 to 14,391 PACS in 2011-2023. Maharashtra has the highest number of PACS (21,059) followed by Gujarat (10,266) and Bihar (8,476). Kerala boasts the highest number of members (2,56,28,261), trailed by Bihar (1,36,29,113) and Tamil Nadu (1,33,39,395). Around 78% PACS (78,489) are affiliated with Federations/ Unions. Out of total 2,69,503 gram panchayats, around 89% (i.e., 2,41,075) panchayats are covered under PACS. Importantly, strengthening PACS involves enhancing their capacity and effectiveness to provide a spectrum of services to farmers and rural communities beyond credit and financial services. Governments and stakeholders aim to uplift rural communities, improve the overall state of agriculture, and foster inclusive economic growth by reinforcing PACS. These efforts will contribute towards reducing poverty, ensuring food security, and promoting sustainable development in agrarian economies. A1. top3.text: 3 PACS Computerisation Project - Guidelines 1 Introduction The Primary Agriculture Credit Societies (PACS) form the vital third tier in the three- tier structure of the Short Term Cooperative Credit Structure (STCCS). The other two tiers are comprised of District Central Cooperative Bank (DCCBs) (2nd tier) and State Cooperative Bank (StCBs) (1st tier). National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development (NABARD), has earlier taken the initiative to bring most of the StCBs and DCCBs on Core Banking Solutions (CBS) platform which has enabled them to give modern-day technology-based banking facilities to their clients. However, the PACS have so far been largely out of the ambit of the technology support. PACS are owned by farmers, rural artisans etc. and aim at promoting thrift and mutual help among the members; cater to their credit requirements and provide credit-linked services like input supply, storage and marketing of agricultural produce etc. DCCBs provide direct linkages to the PACS through direct financing. The StCBs are primarily responsible for control and coordination of the finances of DCCBs. The large out-reach of PACS to the Small and Marginal Farmers (SMFs) make them a systemically important class of agricultural credit purveying institutions. Further, there is a felt need to develop cooperatives as vibrant business enterprises by enabling them to provide multiple services to their members with support of technology in order to fulfil members’ requirements. 49 Sector-wise Cooperatives L ong-term rural credit cooperatives were established for providing funds for investment in agriculture – including land development, farm mechanisation and minor irrigation - rural industries and housing. This structure consists of 14 State Cooperative Agriculture and Rural Development Banks (SCARDBs) operating at the state level and 533 Primary Cooperative Agriculture and Rural Development Banks (PCARDBs) operating at the district/ block level. The structure of long-term rural credit cooperatives differs across states. States like Jammu and Kashmir, Tripura, Uttar Pradesh, Gujarat and Puducherry follow a unitary structure i.e., SCARDBs operate through their own branches with no separate PCARDBs. On the other hand, states like Haryana, Punjab, Rajasthan, Karnataka, Kerala, and Tamil Nadu follow a federal structure wherein SCARDBs lend through PCARDBs. In two states viz., Himachal Pradesh and West Bengal, SCARDBs operate through PCARDBs as well as through their own branches. The business model of SCARDBs and PCARDBs depends heavily on borrowings; the former borrow from institutions such as NABARD for direct lending as well as lending through PCARDBs. The financial health of PCARDBs is, however, more fragile than SCARDBs, given the high share of accumulated losses on their balance sheets. A2. In last two years, since the formation of Ministry of Cooperation, the cooperative movement has been strengthened due to several path-breaking initiatives of the Ministry. One of the initiatives is creation of National Cooperative Database in coordination with States/UTs Government. The comprehensive national database will comprise data of various kinds of cooperatives–from the lowest unit of the cooperative sector, that is, Primary Agricultural Credit Societies (PACS) to national-level institutions. By systematically verifying the grassroots presence of cooperatives, this sector is becoming more streamlined and effective in its operations. This revolutionary initiative not only facilitates the identification of active cooperative societies, but also assists the Government in the formulation of policies to strengthen the cooperative sector to elevate the standard of living for the underprivileged and marginalized sections of society. 2.2 Need for Database Despite India being home to almost 25% of total cooperative societies in the world and with history of cooperative movement in India dating back to more than a century, there was no comprehensive, authentic and updated data repository in the country about cooperatives, their activities, their members, their financial details etc. The availability of organized database of the cooperatives, can help in formulating programs and schemes, mentioning the exact number of beneficiaries. The Ministry of Cooperation was constituted on 6th July, 2021 with a mandate, inter alia to strengthen cooperative movement in the country and deepening its reach up to grassroots; and creation of appropriate policy, legal and institutional framework to help cooperatives realize their potential. To fulfil this mandate, the process for developing a National Cooperative Database was initiated by the Ministry in consultation with the State/UT Governments, National Cooperative Federations, Central line Ministries and all other Stakeholders at various levels. 2.3 Scope & Benefits of National Cooperative Database The objective of developing National Cooperative Database (NCD) is to provide: • A single point access to authentic and updated information on cooperatives of different sectors and develop a process for better understanding of cooperatives. • The database will function as the main planning tool for Central Ministries, State Governments, Cooperative Federations, Cooperators and Sectoral Institutions like NABARD, etc., for cooperative sector. • The database would also bring synergy among various databases maintained by Central line Ministries and State Governments. • It would also help in identifying gaps/ vacuums in geographical distribution of cooperatives in the country and establishing upward/downward linkages of cooperative societies (Primary to Apex). 35 Sector-wise Cooperatives Collectives, including cooperatives, mandate their members to pool in surplus money for onward lending to borrower members. Some of these adhere to the principle of self-help where the products and services are used entirely by their members. Emerging collectives, including credit cooperatives, carry out bulk of their business with non-members. Credit Cooperatives – both banks and credit societies–are the lifeline for all economic activities of members. A strong urban and rural cooperative banking and credit sector can play a catalytic role for growth of cooperatives in various segments of economy. Cooperative banks are basically cooperative societies which are registered under the Cooperative Societies Act of the State concerned or under the Multi-State Cooperative Societies (Amendment) Act, 2023. While cooperative societies functioning within a single state are governed by Cooperative Societies Act of their respective state, cooperative societies functioning in more than one State/ UT are governed by Multi-State Cooperative Societies (Amendment) Act, 2023 under the purview of Government of India. When cooperative societies carry on the business of banking, they come under the regulatory purview of RBI and they are licensed under the provisions of the Banking Regulation Act. The cooperative banking structure in India was developed to complement and supplement the commercial banking structure, with a specific focus on serving the requirements of marginalised borrowers and meeting the development needs of rural as well as urban areas. Urban Cooperative Banks (UCBs) are classified as scheduled and non-scheduled, based on their inclusion or otherwise in the second schedule of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934, and their geographical outreach (single-state or multi-state). Rural cooperatives are segregated by their lending activity, i.e., into short-term vis-à-vis long-term lending. Rural credit short-term credits are channelled through StCB, DCCBs and PACS. Rural long-term credits are disbursed through SCARDBs and PCARDBs. A. Credit Sector Sector-wise Cooperatives

Primary Agricultural Credit Societies (PACS) are village- or panchayat-level cooperative societies that form the lowest tier of the Short-Term Cooperative Credit Structure. PACS deal directly with rural and agricultural borrowers. They provide loans, collect repayment of loans, and may undertake distribution and marketing functions. PACS are an important link between farmers and the higher levels of the cooperative credit system, including District Central Cooperative Banks (DCCBs), State Cooperative Banks (StCBs), and NABARD. --- ## Why are PACS Important? PACS help connect farmers and rural communities with: * Agricultural credit * Farm inputs * Agricultural services * Storage facilities * Markets and distribution * Other cooperative and government-supported services The Ministry of Cooperation describes PACS as the grassroots base of the cooperative credit structure. PACS can help bring farmers closer to credit, agricultural inputs, markets and value addition. --- ## What Services Can PACS Provide? Traditional PACS activities include: * Short-term agricultural credit * Medium-term credit * Distribution of seeds * Distribution of fertilizers * Distribution of pesticides * Storage-related services * Agricultural input services * Marketing and distribution functions * Loan repayment and related credit services Under the Model Bye-laws and diversification initiatives, PACS can also undertake multiple activities beyond traditional credit. These may include: * Dairy activities * Fisheries activities * Floriculture * Food-grain procurement * Warehousing and storage * Fair Price Shops * LPG/CNG/Petrol/Diesel distributorship * Common Service Centre (CSC) services * Business Correspondent or banking-related activities * Insurance-related services * Custom Hiring Centres * Other permitted business activities The exact activities available at an individual PACS depend on its applicable State Cooperative Societies Act, bye-laws, permissions and local implementation. --- ## What Types of Loans Does PACS Provide? PACS traditionally provide: * Short-term agricultural credit * Medium-term agricultural credit The Model Bye-laws and computerization framework also cover financial services involving short-, medium- and long-term loans. However, the exact loan products, limits, interest rates, repayment periods and eligibility conditions depend on the applicable cooperative rules, State provisions and the individual PACS or financing structure. Cooperative banks are basically cooperative societies which are registered under the Cooperative Societies Act of the State concerned or under the Multi-State Cooperative Societies (Amendment) Act, 2023. The cooperative banking structure in India was developed to complement and supplement the commercial banking structure, with a specific focus on serving the requirements of marginalised borrowers and meeting the development needs of rural as well as urban areas. Primary Agricultural Credit Societies (PACS) are village- or panchayat-level cooperative societies that form the lowest tier of the Short-Term Cooperative Credit Structure. PACS deal directly with rural and agricultural borrowers. They provide loans, collect repayment of loans, and may undertake distribution and marketing functions. 36 National Cooperative Database 2023 : A Report P rimary Agriculture Credit Societies (PACS) constitute the lowest tier of the Short-Term Cooperative Credit Structure (STCCS) in the country, primarily providing short-term and medium-term credit facility and other input services, like seed, fertilizer, pesticide distribution, etc. to member farmers. PACS are refinanced by NABARD through District Central Cooperative Banks (DCCBs) and State Cooperative Banks (StCBs). Being the grassroots level cooperative institutions, PACS play a crucial role in sustaining the rural economy of the country by purveying institutional credit to small and marginal farmers. PACS are governed by the Cooperative Acts of their respective states and guided by State Bye-laws. They engage directly with rural (agricultural) borrowers, extending loans, overseeing loan repayments, and managing marketing and distribution functions. Notably, the National Cooperative Database (NCD) portal records the presence of 1,03,304 PACS in the country, with around 95% (i.e., 98,486) of them are being functional in rural areas. Significantly, the growth of PACS has been substantial, expanding from approximately 2,982 PACS in 1900-1923 to 14,391 PACS in 2011-2023. Maharashtra has the highest number of PACS (21,059) followed by Gujarat (10,266) and Bihar (8,476). Kerala boasts the highest number of members (2,56,28,261), trailed by Bihar (1,36,29,113) and Tamil Nadu (1,33,39,395). Around 78% PACS (78,489) are affiliated with Federations/ Unions. Out of total 2,69,503 gram panchayats, around 89% (i.e., 2,41,075) panchayats are covered under PACS. Importantly, strengthening PACS involves enhancing their capacity and effectiveness to provide a spectrum of services to farmers and rural communities beyond credit and financial services. Governments and stakeholders aim to uplift rural communities, improve the overall state of agriculture, and foster inclusive economic growth by reinforcing PACS. These efforts will contribute towards reducing poverty, ensuring food security, and promoting sustainable development in agrarian economies. A1. top3.text: 3 PACS Computerisation Project - Guidelines 1 Introduction The Primary Agriculture Credit Societies (PACS) form the vital third tier in the three- tier structure of the Short Term Cooperative Credit Structure (STCCS). The other two tiers are comprised of District Central Cooperative Bank (DCCBs) (2nd tier) and State Cooperative Bank (StCBs) (1st tier). National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development (NABARD), has earlier taken the initiative to bring most of the StCBs and DCCBs on Core Banking Solutions (CBS) platform which has enabled them to give modern-day technology-based banking facilities to their clients. However, the PACS have so far been largely out of the ambit of the technology support. PACS are owned by farmers, rural artisans etc. and aim at promoting thrift and mutual help among the members; cater to their credit requirements and provide credit-linked services like input supply, storage and marketing of agricultural produce etc. DCCBs provide direct linkages to the PACS through direct financing. The StCBs are primarily responsible for control and coordination of the finances of DCCBs. The large out-reach of PACS to the Small and Marginal Farmers (SMFs) make them a systemically important class of agricultural credit purveying institutions. Further, there is a felt need to develop cooperatives as vibrant business enterprises by enabling them to provide multiple services to their members with support of technology in order to fulfil members’ requirements. Keeping in view the above and to make PACS self-reliant in tune with ‘Atmanirbhar Bharat Abhiyaan’, the Government of India (GoI) has, on 29th June 2022 approved the Centrally Sponsored Project for Computerisation of Primary Agricultural Credit Societies for a period of five years from 2022-23 to 2026-27. 2 Aims & Objectives of the Project The aims and objectives of the project inter alia include the following: a. This structure consists of 14 State Cooperative Agriculture and Rural Development Banks (SCARDBs) operating at the state level and 533 Primary Cooperative Agriculture and Rural Development Banks (PCARDBs) operating at the district/ block level. The structure of long-term rural credit cooperatives differs across states. States like Jammu and Kashmir, Tripura, Uttar Pradesh, Gujarat and Puducherry follow a unitary structure i.e., SCARDBs operate through their own branches with no separate PCARDBs. On the other hand, states like Haryana, Punjab, Rajasthan, Karnataka, Kerala, and Tamil Nadu follow a federal structure wherein SCARDBs lend through PCARDBs. In two states viz., Himachal Pradesh and West Bengal, SCARDBs operate through PCARDBs as well as through their own branches. The business model of SCARDBs and PCARDBs depends heavily on borrowings; the former borrow from institutions such as NABARD for direct lending as well as lending through PCARDBs. The financial health of PCARDBs is, however, more fragile than SCARDBs, given the high share of accumulated losses on their balance sheets. A2. In last two years, since the formation of Ministry of Cooperation, the cooperative movement has been strengthened due to several path-breaking initiatives of the Ministry. One of the initiatives is creation of National Cooperative Database in coordination with States/UTs Government. The comprehensive national database will comprise data of various kinds of cooperatives–from the lowest unit of the cooperative sector, that is, Primary Agricultural Credit Societies (PACS) to national-level institutions. By systematically verifying the grassroots presence of cooperatives, this sector is becoming more streamlined and effective in its operations. This revolutionary initiative not only facilitates the identification of active cooperative societies, but also assists the Government in the formulation of policies to strengthen the cooperative sector to elevate the standard of living for the underprivileged and marginalized sections of society. 2.2 Need for Database Despite India being home to almost 25% of total cooperative societies in the world and with history of cooperative movement in India dating back to more than a century, there was no comprehensive, authentic and updated data repository in the country about cooperatives, their activities, their members, their financial details etc. The availability of organized database of the cooperatives, can help in formulating programs and schemes, mentioning the exact number of beneficiaries. The Ministry of Cooperation was constituted on 6th July, 2021 with a mandate, inter alia to strengthen cooperative movement in the country and deepening its reach up to grassroots; and creation of appropriate policy, legal and institutional framework to help cooperatives realize their potential. To fulfil this mandate, the process for developing a National Cooperative Database was initiated by the Ministry in consultation with the State/UT Governments, National Cooperative Federations, Central line Ministries and all other Stakeholders at various levels. 2.3 Scope & Benefits of National Cooperative Database The objective of developing National Cooperative Database (NCD) is to provide: • A single point access to authentic and updated information on cooperatives of different sectors and develop a process for better understanding of cooperatives. • The database will function as the main planning tool for Central Ministries, State Governments, Cooperative Federations, Cooperators and Sectoral Institutions like NABARD, etc., for cooperative sector. • The database would also bring synergy among various databases maintained by Central line Ministries and State Governments. • It would also help in identifying gaps/ vacuums in geographical distribution of cooperatives in the country and establishing upward/downward linkages of cooperative societies (Primary to Apex). 35 Sector-wise Cooperatives Collectives, including cooperatives, mandate their members to pool in surplus money for onward lending to borrower members. Some of these adhere to the principle of self-help where the products and services are used entirely by their members. Emerging collectives, including credit cooperatives, carry out bulk of their business with non-members. Credit Cooperatives – both banks and credit societies–are the lifeline for all economic activities of members. A strong urban and rural cooperative banking and credit sector can play a catalytic role for growth of cooperatives in various segments of economy. Cooperative banks are basically cooperative societies which are registered under the Cooperative Societies Act of the State concerned or under the Multi-State Cooperative Societies (Amendment) Act, 2023. While cooperative societies functioning within a single state are governed by Cooperative Societies Act of their respective state, cooperative societies functioning in more than one State/ UT are governed by Multi-State Cooperative Societies (Amendment) Act, 2023 under the purview of Government of India. When cooperative societies carry on the business of banking, they come under the regulatory purview of RBI and they are licensed under the provisions of the Banking Regulation Act. The cooperative banking structure in India was developed to complement and supplement the commercial banking structure, with a specific focus on serving the requirements of marginalised borrowers and meeting the development needs of rural as well as urban areas. Urban Cooperative Banks (UCBs) are classified as scheduled and non-scheduled, based on their inclusion or otherwise in the second schedule of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934, and their geographical outreach (single-state or multi-state). Rural cooperatives are segregated by their lending activity, i.e., into short-term vis-à-vis long-term lending. Rural credit short-term credits are channelled through StCB, DCCBs and PACS. Rural long-term credits are disbursed through SCARDBs and PCARDBs. A. Credit Sector Sector-wise Cooperatives

MEMBERSHIP: (1) TYPES OF MEMBERSHIP: The Society shall have two types of membership or types of membership as provided by the State Act/ Rules. “A”-CLASS MEMBERS: ‘A’ class members are the shareholders of the Society who can exercise all the membership rights as provided in the Byelaws. “B”-CLASS MEMBERS: ‘B’ class members are nominal members of the Society. (2) ELIGIBILITY FOR ‘A’ CLASS MEMBERSHIP: The following persons, subject to fulfillment of the eligibility condition, shall be A-Class Members: a) The promoters at the time of registration of Society; b) An Individual who, i) is competent to contract under the provision of Section 11 of the Indian Contract Act 1872 (above 18 years of age, having a sound mind and not debarred by any Law) and ii) possesses agricultural land or land for allied agricultural activities or rearing domestic cattle in the area of operation of the Society; iii) is not a member of any other PACS in any other Panchayat/ Village; (If there is no PACS in the Panchayat/ Village, the members can avail benefits of the nearby PACS after approval of the Registrar) c) State Government or any other Government Body; (3) ELIGIBILITY AND OTHER CONDITIONS FOR ‘B’-CLASS MEMBERSHIP: a) A person who desires to have a business relationship with Society shall be admitted as nominal member by payment of admission fee of Rs.10/- which is non- refundable and shall be credited to Reserve Fund of the Society. b) Self Help Groups/ Joint Liability Groups/ Farmers Interest Groups, Tenant farmers, share croppers, oral lessees or users of land, agricultural labourers, micro entrepreneurs, rural artisans and persons involved in other allied activities shall be admitted as nominal members of the Society.

SIA should verify the current PACS bye-laws before giving a specific membership fee or share requirement. --- ## How Can I Join a PACS? A general PACS membership process may involve: 1. Identify the relevant PACS in the person's area. 2. Check the applicable State cooperative law and PACS bye-laws. 3. Obtain the membership application form or use the available online registration facility, where implemented. 4. Complete the required KYC and submit the required documents. 5. Submit identity, residence, land-holding or other applicable proof as required. 6. Pay the applicable admission fee and share contribution, if required. 7. The application may be placed before the Board of Directors for a decision according to the applicable bye-laws. 8. If approved, complete the remaining membership formalities. Under the Model Bye-laws, the Board of Directors decides the membership application within the prescribed period, and the applicant is informed of the decision according to the applicable procedure. Yes. PACS directly deal with rural and agricultural borrowers and provide credit. PACS traditionally provide short-term and medium-term agricultural credit to member farmers. Loan availability, amount, interest rate, repayment period, collateral requirements and eligibility depend on the applicable rules and the concerned cooperative credit institution. SIA should verify current loan conditions before giving specific financial figures. --- ## What Agricultural Inputs Can PACS Provide? PACS may provide or distribute agricultural inputs such as: * Seeds * Fertilizers * Pesticides They may also provide other agricultural services depending on their activities and applicable rules. --- ## Can PACS Provide Storage Services? Yes. PACS can undertake storage and warehousing-related activities. The Model Bye-laws support diversification of PACS into activities such as godowns, warehousing and food-grain procurement. Individual availability depends on the PACS, local implementation and applicable permissions. --- ## Can PACS Function as Common Service Centres? Yes. The Ministry of Cooperation has enabled PACS to function as Common Service Centres (CSCs). Through the CSC framework, PACS can provide various e-governance and citizen-centric services. These

top3.text: 3 PACS Computerisation Project - Guidelines 1 Introduction The Primary Agriculture Credit Societies (PACS) form the vital third tier in the three- tier structure of the Short Term Cooperative Credit Structure (STCCS). The other two tiers are comprised of District Central Cooperative Bank (DCCBs) (2nd tier) and State Cooperative Bank (StCBs) (1st tier). National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development (NABARD), has earlier taken the initiative to bring most of the StCBs and DCCBs on Core Banking Solutions (CBS) platform which has enabled them to give modern-day technology-based banking facilities to their clients. However, the PACS have so far been largely out of the ambit of the technology support. PACS are owned by farmers, rural artisans etc. and aim at promoting thrift and mutual help among the members; cater to their credit requirements and provide credit-linked services like input supply, storage and marketing of agricultural produce etc. DCCBs provide direct linkages to the PACS through direct financing. The StCBs are primarily responsible for control and coordination of the finances of DCCBs. The large out-reach of PACS to the Small and Marginal Farmers (SMFs) make them a systemically important class of agricultural credit purveying institutions. Further, there is a felt need to develop cooperatives as vibrant business enterprises by enabling them to provide multiple services to their members with support of technology in order to fulfil members’ requirements. Primary Agricultural Credit Societies (PACS) are village- or panchayat-level cooperative societies that form the lowest tier of the Short-Term Cooperative Credit Structure. PACS deal directly with rural and agricultural borrowers. They provide loans, collect repayment of loans, and may undertake distribution and marketing functions. PACS are an important link between farmers and the higher levels of the cooperative credit system, including District Central Cooperative Banks (DCCBs), State Cooperative Banks (StCBs), and NABARD. --- ## Why are PACS Important? PACS help connect farmers and rural communities with: * Agricultural credit * Farm inputs * Agricultural services * Storage facilities * Markets and distribution * Other cooperative and government-supported services The Ministry of Cooperation describes PACS as the grassroots base of the cooperative credit structure. PACS can help bring farmers closer to credit, agricultural inputs, markets and value addition. --- ## What Services Can PACS Provide? Traditional PACS activities include: * Short-term agricultural credit * Medium-term credit * Distribution of seeds * Distribution of fertilizers * Distribution of pesticides * Storage-related services * Agricultural input services * Marketing and distribution functions * Loan repayment and related credit services Under the Model Bye-laws and diversification initiatives, PACS can also undertake multiple activities beyond traditional credit. These may include: * Dairy activities * Fisheries activities * Floriculture * Food-grain procurement * Warehousing and storage * Fair Price Shops * LPG/CNG/Petrol/Diesel distributorship * Common Service Centre (CSC) services * Business Correspondent or banking-related activities * Insurance-related services * Custom Hiring Centres * Other permitted business activities The exact activities available at an individual PACS depend on its applicable State Cooperative Societies Act, bye-laws, permissions and local implementation. --- ## What Types of Loans Does PACS Provide? PACS traditionally provide: * Short-term agricultural credit * Medium-term agricultural credit The Model Bye-laws and computerization framework also cover financial services involving short-, medium- and long-term loans. However, the exact loan products, limits, interest rates, repayment periods and eligibility conditions depend on the applicable cooperative rules, State provisions and the individual PACS or financing structure. 36 National Cooperative Database 2023 : A Report P rimary Agriculture Credit Societies (PACS) constitute the lowest tier of the Short-Term Cooperative Credit Structure (STCCS) in the country, primarily providing short-term and medium-term credit facility and other input services, like seed, fertilizer, pesticide distribution, etc. to member farmers. PACS are refinanced by NABARD through District Central Cooperative Banks (DCCBs) and State Cooperative Banks (StCBs). Being the grassroots level cooperative institutions, PACS play a crucial role in sustaining the rural economy of the country by purveying institutional credit to small and marginal farmers. PACS are governed by the Cooperative Acts of their respective states and guided by State Bye-laws. They engage directly with rural (agricultural) borrowers, extending loans, overseeing loan repayments, and managing marketing and distribution functions. Notably, the National Cooperative Database (NCD) portal records the presence of 1,03,304 PACS in the country, with around 95% (i.e., 98,486) of them are being functional in rural areas. Significantly, the growth of PACS has been substantial, expanding from approximately 2,982 PACS in 1900-1923 to 14,391 PACS in 2011-2023. Maharashtra has the highest number of PACS (21,059) followed by Gujarat (10,266) and Bihar (8,476). Kerala boasts the highest number of members (2,56,28,261), trailed by Bihar (1,36,29,113) and Tamil Nadu (1,33,39,395). Around 78% PACS (78,489) are affiliated with Federations/ Unions. Out of total 2,69,503 gram panchayats, around 89% (i.e., 2,41,075) panchayats are covered under PACS. Importantly, strengthening PACS involves enhancing their capacity and effectiveness to provide a spectrum of services to farmers and rural communities beyond credit and financial services. Governments and stakeholders aim to uplift rural communities, improve the overall state of agriculture, and foster inclusive economic growth by reinforcing PACS. These efforts will contribute towards reducing poverty, ensuring food security, and promoting sustainable development in agrarian economies. A1. The PACS receives applicable margins and incentives subject to the scheme guidelines. ## FAQs / Query Intents ### What is a Jan Aushadhi Kendra by PACS? It is a Pradhan Mantri Bhartiya Janaushadhi Kendra operated by a Primary Agricultural Credit Society (PACS). ### Can PACS open Jan Aushadhi Kendras? Yes. PACS can be allowed to open and operate Jan Aushadhi Kendras subject to the applicable Government procedures and conditions. ### Why are Jan Aushadhi Kendras being promoted through PACS? The initiative improves access to affordable medicines in rural areas and provides PACS with an additional economic activity. ### What are the benefits for PACS? PACS operating Jan Aushadhi Kendras can receive applicable trade margins and incentives under the PMBJP framework, subject to current guidelines. ### How many Jan Aushadhi Kendras have been opened through PACS? As of 30 June 2026, 846 Jan Aushadhi Kendras had been opened under PACS across the country. ### How many PACS have received initial approval? As of 30 June 2026, more than 4,250 PACS had received initial approval to open Jan Aushadhi Kendras. ### Is there a State-wise target for PACS Jan Aushadhi Kendras? No. As of the latest official information, there is no State/UT/District-wise target for opening new Jan Aushadhi Kendras through PACS. ### What is the target for Jan Aushadhi Kendras? ICDP stands for Integrated Cooperative Development Projects. It is a cooperative development framework used to support integrated development of cooperative institutions and activities in identified areas. ### What does ICDP stand for? ICDP stands for Integrated Cooperative Development Projects. ### What is the main purpose of ICDP? Its main purpose is to strengthen cooperative institutions and support infrastructure, capacity building and economic activities through integrated cooperative development projects. ### Who can benefit from ICDP? Eligible cooperative societies, cooperative institutions, cooperative members and communities served by the cooperatives may benefit according to the approved project. ### What type of support can ICDP provide? Depending on the project, support may include infrastructure development, financial assistance for approved activities, training, capacity building and institutional strengthening. ### Does ICDP support cooperative infrastructure? Yes. Approved ICDP projects may support infrastructure such as storage, processing, marketing and other cooperative facilities. ### Does ICDP support farmers? Farmers may benefit indirectly or directly through eligible cooperative institutions and services supported by an approved ICDP project. ### Is ICDP an individual cash-benefit scheme? No. ICDP is primarily a cooperative development project framework rather than a general individual cash-benefit scheme. ### Can a cooperative society participate in ICDP? Eligible cooperative societies may participate through approved ICDP projects according to the applicable project and government arrangements. ### Where can a cooperative get information about ICDP? A cooperative can approach the State cooperative department, district cooperative authority, relevant cooperative federation, designated implementing agency or Ministry of Cooperation. ### Is ICDP available across India? ICDP projects are undertaken in identified areas according to applicable government planning and approval arrangements. Availability and implementation can therefore vary by project and location. ### Are ICDP benefits the same for every project? No. The activities, support and beneficiaries depend on the approved project and applicable government provisions. ## Important Note ICDP should not be presented as a single uniform individual subsidy

मतिान करने की अनुमजत िी िाएगी । ऐसी ििा में भुगतान की गई आपजत्त फीस िब् त कर ली िाएगी । (10) मतिान के अंत में ररटर्नंग अजधकारी एकजत्रत आपजत्त फीस, आपजत्त करने वाले ्‍ यजियों को वापस की गई फीस और िब् त की गई फीस का जहसाब तैयार करेगा और साथ में प्रत् येक मामले में संजिप् त िांच के पश् चातम उसके द्वारा जलए गए जनणायों का संजिप् त सार सोसाइटी को िेगा । (11) यदि मतिान के दकसी चरण में, िंगा या हंगामा द्वारा कायावाही अवरुद्ध या बाजधत होती है या यदि ऐसे जनवााचन में दकसी पयााप् त कारणों से मतिान कराना संभव नहीं है तो ररटर्नंग अजधकारी को मतिान रे करने के ऐसे कारणों को अजभलेजखत करने के पश् चातम, मतिान रे करने की िजि होगी । (12) मतिान के जलए जनयत समय के पश् चातम दकसी मतिाता को मतिान करने की अनुमजत नहीं िी िाएगी । परंतु दक यदि कोई मतिाता, मतिान के समय की समाजप्त के पूवा पररसर में प्रवेि कर चुका हो तो उसे मतपत्र िारी कर मतिान करने की अनुमजत िी िाएगी । (13) मतिान की समाजप्त के ीक पश् चातम मतगणना आरंभ की िाएगी और यदि ररटर्नंग अजधकारी के जनयंत्रण से परे यदि मतों की गणना तुरंत संभव नहीं है तो मतपेटी को ररटर्नंग अजधकारी और जनवााचन में खड़े अभ् यर्थायों या उनके एिेंटों के मुहरों से मुहरबंि कर दिया िाएगा, और यदि यह उनकी इच् छा हो तो मतपेरटयां सोसाइटी की सुरजित अजभरिा में िमा कर िी िाएगी और ऐसी जस्ट्थजत में ररटर्नंग अजधकारी अगले दिन आरंभ होने वाली मतगणना का स्ट् थान और समय की घोिणा करेगा और अभ् यथी और उसके अजभकतााओं को जलजखत में भी सूजचत करेगा और मतगणना अगले दिन ररटर्नंग अजधकारी द्वारा या उसके पयावेिण में की िाएगी और प्रत् येक अभ् यथी और उनके प्राजधकृत अजभकताा को मतगणना के समय उपजस्ट्थत रहने का अजधकार होगा तथा दकसी अभ् यथी या उसके अजभकताा के मतगणना में अनुपजस्ट्थत रहने से ररटर्नंग अजधकारी द्वारा मतगणना या पररणाम की घोिणा जनष् प्रभावी नहीं होगी । (14) ररटर्नंग अजधकारी द्वारा मतगणना की समाजप्त के पश् चातम, वह मतिान के पररणाम की एक जववरणी तैयार करेगा और प्राजधकरण के पूवाानुमोिन से तुरंत पररणाम घोजित करेगा ।

Primary Agricultural Credit Societies (PACS) are village- or panchayat-level cooperative societies that form the lowest tier of the Short-Term Cooperative Credit Structure. PACS deal directly with rural and agricultural borrowers. They provide loans, collect repayment of loans, and may undertake distribution and marketing functions. PACS are an important link between farmers and the higher levels of the cooperative credit system, including District Central Cooperative Banks (DCCBs), State Cooperative Banks (StCBs), and NABARD. --- ## Why are PACS Important? PACS help connect farmers and rural communities with: * Agricultural credit * Farm inputs * Agricultural services * Storage facilities * Markets and distribution * Other cooperative and government-supported services The Ministry of Cooperation describes PACS as the grassroots base of the cooperative credit structure. PACS can help bring farmers closer to credit, agricultural inputs, markets and value addition. --- ## What Services Can PACS Provide? Traditional PACS activities include: * Short-term agricultural credit * Medium-term credit * Distribution of seeds * Distribution of fertilizers * Distribution of pesticides * Storage-related services * Agricultural input services * Marketing and distribution functions * Loan repayment and related credit services Under the Model Bye-laws and diversification initiatives, PACS can also undertake multiple activities beyond traditional credit. These may include: * Dairy activities * Fisheries activities * Floriculture * Food-grain procurement * Warehousing and storage * Fair Price Shops * LPG/CNG/Petrol/Diesel distributorship * Common Service Centre (CSC) services * Business Correspondent or banking-related activities * Insurance-related services * Custom Hiring Centres * Other permitted business activities The exact activities available at an individual PACS depend on its applicable State Cooperative Societies Act, bye-laws, permissions and local implementation. --- ## What Types of Loans Does PACS Provide? PACS traditionally provide: * Short-term agricultural credit * Medium-term agricultural credit The Model Bye-laws and computerization framework also cover financial services involving short-, medium- and long-term loans. However, the exact loan products, limits, interest rates, repayment periods and eligibility conditions depend on the applicable cooperative rules, State provisions and the individual PACS or financing structure. 36 National Cooperative Database 2023 : A Report P rimary Agriculture Credit Societies (PACS) constitute the lowest tier of the Short-Term Cooperative Credit Structure (STCCS) in the country, primarily providing short-term and medium-term credit facility and other input services, like seed, fertilizer, pesticide distribution, etc. to member farmers. PACS are refinanced by NABARD through District Central Cooperative Banks (DCCBs) and State Cooperative Banks (StCBs). Being the grassroots level cooperative institutions, PACS play a crucial role in sustaining the rural economy of the country by purveying institutional credit to small and marginal farmers. PACS are governed by the Cooperative Acts of their respective states and guided by State Bye-laws. They engage directly with rural (agricultural) borrowers, extending loans, overseeing loan repayments, and managing marketing and distribution functions. Notably, the National Cooperative Database (NCD) portal records the presence of 1,03,304 PACS in the country, with around 95% (i.e., 98,486) of them are being functional in rural areas. Significantly, the growth of PACS has been substantial, expanding from approximately 2,982 PACS in 1900-1923 to 14,391 PACS in 2011-2023. Maharashtra has the highest number of PACS (21,059) followed by Gujarat (10,266) and Bihar (8,476). Kerala boasts the highest number of members (2,56,28,261), trailed by Bihar (1,36,29,113) and Tamil Nadu (1,33,39,395). Around 78% PACS (78,489) are affiliated with Federations/ Unions. Out of total 2,69,503 gram panchayats, around 89% (i.e., 2,41,075) panchayats are covered under PACS. Importantly, strengthening PACS involves enhancing their capacity and effectiveness to provide a spectrum of services to farmers and rural communities beyond credit and financial services. Governments and stakeholders aim to uplift rural communities, improve the overall state of agriculture, and foster inclusive economic growth by reinforcing PACS. These efforts will contribute towards reducing poverty, ensuring food security, and promoting sustainable development in agrarian economies. A1. top3.text: 3 PACS Computerisation Project - Guidelines 1 Introduction The Primary Agriculture Credit Societies (PACS) form the vital third tier in the three- tier structure of the Short Term Cooperative Credit Structure (STCCS). The other two tiers are comprised of District Central Cooperative Bank (DCCBs) (2nd tier) and State Cooperative Bank (StCBs) (1st tier). National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development (NABARD), has earlier taken the initiative to bring most of the StCBs and DCCBs on Core Banking Solutions (CBS) platform which has enabled them to give modern-day technology-based banking facilities to their clients. However, the PACS have so far been largely out of the ambit of the technology support. PACS are owned by farmers, rural artisans etc. and aim at promoting thrift and mutual help among the members; cater to their credit requirements and provide credit-linked services like input supply, storage and marketing of agricultural produce etc. DCCBs provide direct linkages to the PACS through direct financing. The StCBs are primarily responsible for control and coordination of the finances of DCCBs. The large out-reach of PACS to the Small and Marginal Farmers (SMFs) make them a systemically important class of agricultural credit purveying institutions. Further, there is a felt need to develop cooperatives as vibrant business enterprises by enabling them to provide multiple services to their members with support of technology in order to fulfil members’ requirements. Keeping in view the above and to make PACS self-reliant in tune with ‘Atmanirbhar Bharat Abhiyaan’, the Government of India (GoI) has, on 29th June 2022 approved the Centrally Sponsored Project for Computerisation of Primary Agricultural Credit Societies for a period of five years from 2022-23 to 2026-27. 2 Aims & Objectives of the Project The aims and objectives of the project inter alia include the following: a. 49 Sector-wise Cooperatives L ong-term rural credit cooperatives were established for providing funds for investment in agriculture – including land development, farm mechanisation and minor irrigation - rural industries and housing. This structure consists of 14 State Cooperative Agriculture and Rural Development Banks (SCARDBs) operating at the state level and 533 Primary Cooperative Agriculture and Rural Development Banks (PCARDBs) operating at the district/ block level. The structure of long-term rural credit cooperatives differs across states. States like Jammu and Kashmir, Tripura, Uttar Pradesh, Gujarat and Puducherry follow a unitary structure i.e., SCARDBs operate through their own branches with no separate PCARDBs. On the other hand, states like Haryana, Punjab, Rajasthan, Karnataka, Kerala, and Tamil Nadu follow a federal structure wherein SCARDBs lend through PCARDBs. In two states viz., Himachal Pradesh and West Bengal, SCARDBs operate through PCARDBs as well as through their own branches. The business model of SCARDBs and PCARDBs depends heavily on borrowings; the former borrow from institutions such as NABARD for direct lending as well as lending through PCARDBs. The financial health of PCARDBs is, however, more fragile than SCARDBs, given the high share of accumulated losses on their balance sheets. A2. A strong urban and rural cooperative banking and credit sector can play a catalytic role for growth of cooperatives in various segments of economy. Cooperative banks are basically cooperative societies which are registered under the Cooperative Societies Act of the State concerned or under the Multi-State Cooperative Societies (Amendment) Act, 2023. While cooperative societies functioning within a single state are governed by Cooperative Societies Act of their respective state, cooperative societies functioning in more than one State/ UT are governed by Multi-State Cooperative Societies (Amendment) Act, 2023 under the purview of Government of India. When cooperative societies carry on the business of banking, they come under the regulatory purview of RBI and they are licensed under the provisions of the Banking Regulation Act. The cooperative banking structure in India was developed to complement and supplement the commercial banking structure, with a specific focus on serving the requirements of marginalised borrowers and meeting the development needs of rural as well as urban areas. Urban Cooperative Banks (UCBs) are classified as scheduled and non-scheduled, based on their inclusion or otherwise in the second schedule of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934, and their geographical outreach (single-state or multi-state). Rural cooperatives are segregated by their lending activity, i.e., into short-term vis-à-vis long-term lending. Rural credit short-term credits are channelled through StCB, DCCBs and PACS. PACS deal directly with rural and agricultural borrowers. They provide loans, collect repayment of loans, and may undertake distribution and marketing functions. 36 National Cooperative Database 2023 : A Report P rimary Agriculture Credit Societies (PACS) constitute the lowest tier of the Short-Term Cooperative Credit Structure (STCCS) in the country, primarily providing short-term and medium-term credit facility and other input services, like seed, fertilizer, pesticide distribution, etc. to member farmers. PACS are refinanced by NABARD through District Central Cooperative Banks (DCCBs) and State Cooperative Banks (StCBs). Being the grassroots level cooperative institutions, PACS play a crucial role in sustaining the rural economy of the country by purveying institutional credit to small and marginal farmers. PACS are governed by the Cooperative Acts of their respective states and guided by State Bye-laws. They engage directly with rural (agricultural) borrowers, extending loans, overseeing loan repayments, and managing marketing and distribution functions. Notably, the National Cooperative Database (NCD) portal records the presence of 1,03,304 PACS in the country, with around 95% (i.e., 98,486) of them are being functional in rural areas. Significantly, the growth of PACS has been substantial, expanding from approximately 2,982 PACS in 1900-1923 to 14,391 PACS in 2011-2023. Maharashtra has the highest number of PACS (21,059) followed by Gujarat (10,266) and Bihar (8,476). Kerala boasts the highest number of members (2,56,28,261), trailed by Bihar (1,36,29,113) and Tamil Nadu (1,33,39,395). Around 78% PACS (78,489) are affiliated with Federations/ Unions. Out of total 2,69,503 gram panchayats, around 89% (i.e., 2,41,075) panchayats are covered under PACS. Importantly, strengthening PACS involves enhancing their capacity and effectiveness to provide a spectrum of services to farmers and rural communities beyond credit and financial services. Governments and stakeholders aim to uplift rural communities, improve the overall state of agriculture, and foster inclusive economic growth by reinforcing PACS. These efforts will contribute towards reducing poverty, ensuring food security, and promoting sustainable development in agrarian economies. A1. top3.text: 3 PACS Computerisation Project - Guidelines 1 Introduction The Primary Agriculture Credit Societies (PACS) form the vital third tier in the three- tier structure of the Short Term Cooperative Credit Structure (STCCS). The other two tiers are comprised of District Central Cooperative Bank (DCCBs) (2nd tier) and State Cooperative Bank (StCBs) (1st tier). National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development (NABARD), has earlier taken the initiative to bring most of the StCBs and DCCBs on Core Banking Solutions (CBS) platform which has enabled them to give modern-day technology-based banking facilities to their clients. However, the PACS have so far been largely out of the ambit of the technology support. PACS are owned by farmers, rural artisans etc. and aim at promoting thrift and mutual help among the members; cater to their credit requirements and provide credit-linked services like input supply, storage and marketing of agricultural produce etc. DCCBs provide direct linkages to the PACS through direct financing. The StCBs are primarily responsible for control and coordination of the finances of DCCBs. The large out-reach of PACS to the Small and Marginal Farmers (SMFs) make them a systemically important class of agricultural credit purveying institutions. Further, there is a felt need to develop cooperatives as vibrant business enterprises by enabling them to provide multiple services to their members with support of technology in order to fulfil members’ requirements. Keeping in view the above and to make PACS self-reliant in tune with ‘Atmanirbhar Bharat Abhiyaan’, the Government of India (GoI) has, on 29th June 2022 approved the Centrally Sponsored Project for Computerisation of Primary Agricultural Credit Societies for a period of five years from 2022-23 to 2026-27. 2 Aims & Objectives of the Project The aims and objectives of the project inter alia include the following: a. The structure of long-term rural credit cooperatives differs across states. States like Jammu and Kashmir, Tripura, Uttar Pradesh, Gujarat and Puducherry follow a unitary structure i.e., SCARDBs operate through their own branches with no separate PCARDBs. On the other hand, states like Haryana, Punjab, Rajasthan, Karnataka, Kerala, and Tamil Nadu follow a federal structure wherein SCARDBs lend through PCARDBs. In two states viz., Himachal Pradesh and West Bengal, SCARDBs operate through PCARDBs as well as through their own branches. The business model of SCARDBs and PCARDBs depends heavily on borrowings; the former borrow from institutions such as NABARD for direct lending as well as lending through PCARDBs. The financial health of PCARDBs is, however, more fragile than SCARDBs, given the high share of accumulated losses on their balance sheets. A2. 45 Sector-wise Cooperatives A State’s three-tier rural cooperative credit structure consists of State Cooperative Banks (StCBs), District Central Cooperative Banks (DCCBs), and Primary Agricultural Credit Societies (PACS), which concentrate on agricultural and rural development. State cooperative banks are the apex institutions in this structure. The National Cooperative Database (NCD) records the presence of 32 registered State Cooperative Banks in the country except for 5 States/UTs namely Haryana, Ladakh, Lakshadweep, Manipur, and Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu. These cooperative banks offer a comprehensive range of services, from savings accounts to agricultural loans, actively supporting priority sectors and contributing to the well-being of local communities. With a clear mandate to promote financial inclusion and bolster essential sectors like agriculture and small-scale industries, cooperative banks remain instrumental in fostering economic growth and meeting the diverse needs of India’s population. 4.3 State Cooperative Bank (SCBs)

35 Sector-wise Cooperatives Collectives, including cooperatives, mandate their members to pool in surplus money for onward lending to borrower members. Some of these adhere to the principle of self-help where the products and services are used entirely by their members. Emerging collectives, including credit cooperatives, carry out bulk of their business with non-members. Credit Cooperatives – both banks and credit societies–are the lifeline for all economic activities of members. A strong urban and rural cooperative banking and credit sector can play a catalytic role for growth of cooperatives in various segments of economy. Cooperative banks are basically cooperative societies which are registered under the Cooperative Societies Act of the State concerned or under the Multi-State Cooperative Societies (Amendment) Act, 2023. While cooperative societies functioning within a single state are governed by Cooperative Societies Act of their respective state, cooperative societies functioning in more than one State/ UT are governed by Multi-State Cooperative Societies (Amendment) Act, 2023 under the purview of Government of India. When cooperative societies carry on the business of banking, they come under the regulatory purview of RBI and they are licensed under the provisions of the Banking Regulation Act. The cooperative banking structure in India was developed to complement and supplement the commercial banking structure, with a specific focus on serving the requirements of marginalised borrowers and meeting the development needs of rural as well as urban areas. Urban Cooperative Banks (UCBs) are classified as scheduled and non-scheduled, based on their inclusion or otherwise in the second schedule of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934, and their geographical outreach (single-state or multi-state). Rural cooperatives are segregated by their lending activity, i.e., into short-term vis-à-vis long-term lending. Rural credit short-term credits are channelled through StCB, DCCBs and PACS. Rural long-term credits are disbursed through SCARDBs and PCARDBs. A. Credit Sector Sector-wise Cooperatives

In last two years, since the formation of Ministry of Cooperation, the cooperative movement has been strengthened due to several path-breaking initiatives of the Ministry. One of the initiatives is creation of National Cooperative Database in coordination with States/UTs Government. The comprehensive national database will comprise data of various kinds of cooperatives–from the lowest unit of the cooperative sector, that is, Primary Agricultural Credit Societies (PACS) to national-level institutions. By systematically verifying the grassroots presence of cooperatives, this sector is becoming more streamlined and effective in its operations. This revolutionary initiative not only facilitates the identification of active cooperative societies, but also assists the Government in the formulation of policies to strengthen the cooperative sector to elevate the standard of living for the underprivileged and marginalized sections of society. 2.2 Need for Database Despite India being home to almost 25% of total cooperative societies in the world and with history of cooperative movement in India dating back to more than a century, there was no comprehensive, authentic and updated data repository in the country about cooperatives, their activities, their members, their financial details etc. The availability of organized database of the cooperatives, can help in formulating programs and schemes, mentioning the exact number of beneficiaries. The Ministry of Cooperation was constituted on 6th July, 2021 with a mandate, inter alia to strengthen cooperative movement in the country and deepening its reach up to grassroots; and creation of appropriate policy, legal and institutional framework to help cooperatives realize their potential. To fulfil this mandate, the process for developing a National Cooperative Database was initiated by the Ministry in consultation with the State/UT Governments, National Cooperative Federations, Central line Ministries and all other Stakeholders at various levels. 2.3 Scope & Benefits of National Cooperative Database The objective of developing National Cooperative Database (NCD) is to provide: • A single point access to authentic and updated information on cooperatives of different sectors and develop a process for better understanding of cooperatives. • The database will function as the main planning tool for Central Ministries, State Governments, Cooperative Federations, Cooperators and Sectoral Institutions like NABARD, etc., for cooperative sector. • The database would also bring synergy among various databases maintained by Central line Ministries and State Governments. • It would also help in identifying gaps/ vacuums in geographical distribution of cooperatives in the country and establishing upward/downward linkages of cooperative societies (Primary to Apex). Primary Agricultural Credit Societies (PACS) are village- or panchayat-level cooperative societies that form the lowest tier of the Short-Term Cooperative Credit Structure. PACS deal directly with rural and agricultural borrowers. They provide loans, collect repayment of loans, and may undertake distribution and marketing functions. PACS are an important link between farmers and the higher levels of the cooperative credit system, including District Central Cooperative Banks (DCCBs), State Cooperative Banks (StCBs), and NABARD. --- ## Why are PACS Important? PACS help connect farmers and rural communities with: * Agricultural credit * Farm inputs * Agricultural services * Storage facilities * Markets and distribution * Other cooperative and government-supported services The Ministry of Cooperation describes PACS as the grassroots base of the cooperative credit structure. PACS can help bring farmers closer to credit, agricultural inputs, markets and value addition. --- ## What Services Can PACS Provide? PACS traditionally provide: * Short-term agricultural credit * Medium-term agricultural credit The Model Bye-laws and computerization framework also cover financial services involving short-, medium- and long-term loans. However, the exact loan products, limits, interest rates, repayment periods and eligibility conditions depend on the applicable cooperative rules, State provisions and the individual PACS or financing structure. 36 National Cooperative Database 2023 : A Report P rimary Agriculture Credit Societies (PACS) constitute the lowest tier of the Short-Term Cooperative Credit Structure (STCCS) in the country, primarily providing short-term and medium-term credit facility and other input services, like seed, fertilizer, pesticide distribution, etc. to member farmers. PACS are refinanced by NABARD through District Central Cooperative Banks (DCCBs) and State Cooperative Banks (StCBs). Being the grassroots level cooperative institutions, PACS play a crucial role in sustaining the rural economy of the country by purveying institutional credit to small and marginal farmers. PACS are governed by the Cooperative Acts of their respective states and guided by State Bye-laws. They engage directly with rural (agricultural) borrowers, extending loans, overseeing loan repayments, and managing marketing and distribution functions. Notably, the National Cooperative Database (NCD) portal records the presence of 1,03,304 PACS in the country, with around 95% (i.e., 98,486) of them are being functional in rural areas. Significantly, the growth of PACS has been substantial, expanding from approximately 2,982 PACS in 1900-1923 to 14,391 PACS in 2011-2023. Maharashtra has the highest number of PACS (21,059) followed by Gujarat (10,266) and Bihar (8,476). Kerala boasts the highest number of members (2,56,28,261), trailed by Bihar (1,36,29,113) and Tamil Nadu (1,33,39,395). Around 78% PACS (78,489) are affiliated with Federations/ Unions. Out of total 2,69,503 gram panchayats, around 89% (i.e., 2,41,075) panchayats are covered under PACS. Importantly, strengthening PACS involves enhancing their capacity and effectiveness to provide a spectrum of services to farmers and rural communities beyond credit and financial services. Governments and stakeholders aim to uplift rural communities, improve the overall state of agriculture, and foster inclusive economic growth by reinforcing PACS. These efforts will contribute towards reducing poverty, ensuring food security, and promoting sustainable development in agrarian economies. A1. The structure of long-term rural credit cooperatives differs across states. States like Jammu and Kashmir, Tripura, Uttar Pradesh, Gujarat and Puducherry follow a unitary structure i.e., SCARDBs operate through their own branches with no separate PCARDBs. On the other hand, states like Haryana, Punjab, Rajasthan, Karnataka, Kerala, and Tamil Nadu follow a federal structure wherein SCARDBs lend through PCARDBs. In two states viz., Himachal Pradesh and West Bengal, SCARDBs operate through PCARDBs as well as through their own branches. The business model of SCARDBs and PCARDBs depends heavily on borrowings; the former borrow from institutions such as NABARD for direct lending as well as lending through PCARDBs. Some of these adhere to the principle of self-help where the products and services are used entirely by their members. Emerging collectives, including credit cooperatives, carry out bulk of their business with non-members. Credit Cooperatives – both banks and credit societies–are the lifeline for all economic activities of members. A strong urban and rural cooperative banking and credit sector can play a catalytic role for growth of cooperatives in various segments of economy. Cooperative banks are basically cooperative societies which are registered under the Cooperative Societies Act of the State concerned or under the Multi-State Cooperative Societies (Amendment) Act, 2023. While cooperative societies functioning within a single state are governed by Cooperative Societies Act of their respective state, cooperative societies functioning in more than one State/ UT are governed by Multi-State Cooperative Societies (Amendment) Act, 2023 under the purview of Government of India. When cooperative societies carry on the business of banking, they come under the regulatory purview of RBI and they are licensed under the provisions of the Banking Regulation Act. The cooperative banking structure in India was developed to complement and supplement the commercial banking structure, with a specific focus on serving the requirements of marginalised borrowers and meeting the development needs of rural as well as urban areas. Urban Cooperative Banks (UCBs) are classified as scheduled and non-scheduled, based on their inclusion or otherwise in the second schedule of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934, and their geographical outreach (single-state or multi-state). Rural cooperatives are segregated by their lending activity, i.e., into short-term vis-à-vis long-term lending. Rural credit short-term credits are channelled through StCB, DCCBs and PACS. Rural long-term credits are disbursed through SCARDBs and PCARDBs. A. Credit Sector Sector-wise Cooperatives

Primary Agricultural Credit Societies (PACS) are village- or panchayat-level cooperative societies that form the lowest tier of the Short-Term Cooperative Credit Structure. PACS deal directly with rural and agricultural borrowers. They provide loans, collect repayment of loans, and may undertake distribution and marketing functions. PACS are an important link between farmers and the higher levels of the cooperative credit system, including District Central Cooperative Banks (DCCBs), State Cooperative Banks (StCBs), and NABARD. --- ## Why are PACS Important? PACS help connect farmers and rural communities with: * Agricultural credit * Farm inputs * Agricultural services * Storage facilities * Markets and distribution * Other cooperative and government-supported services The Ministry of Cooperation describes PACS as the grassroots base of the cooperative credit structure. PACS can help bring farmers closer to credit, agricultural inputs, markets and value addition. --- ## What Services Can PACS Provide? Traditional PACS activities include: * Short-term agricultural credit * Medium-term credit * Distribution of seeds * Distribution of fertilizers * Distribution of pesticides * Storage-related services * Agricultural input services * Marketing and distribution functions * Loan repayment and related credit services Under the Model Bye-laws and diversification initiatives, PACS can also undertake multiple activities beyond traditional credit. These may include: * Dairy activities * Fisheries activities * Floriculture * Food-grain procurement * Warehousing and storage * Fair Price Shops * LPG/CNG/Petrol/Diesel distributorship * Common Service Centre (CSC) services * Business Correspondent or banking-related activities * Insurance-related services * Custom Hiring Centres * Other permitted business activities The exact activities available at an individual PACS depend on its applicable State Cooperative Societies Act, bye-laws, permissions and local implementation. --- ## What Types of Loans Does PACS Provide? PACS traditionally provide: * Short-term agricultural credit * Medium-term agricultural credit The Model Bye-laws and computerization framework also cover financial services involving short-, medium- and long-term loans. However, the exact loan products, limits, interest rates, repayment periods and eligibility conditions depend on the applicable cooperative rules, State provisions and the individual PACS or financing structure. 36 National Cooperative Database 2023 : A Report P rimary Agriculture Credit Societies (PACS) constitute the lowest tier of the Short-Term Cooperative Credit Structure (STCCS) in the country, primarily providing short-term and medium-term credit facility and other input services, like seed, fertilizer, pesticide distribution, etc. to member farmers. PACS are refinanced by NABARD through District Central Cooperative Banks (DCCBs) and State Cooperative Banks (StCBs). Being the grassroots level cooperative institutions, PACS play a crucial role in sustaining the rural economy of the country by purveying institutional credit to small and marginal farmers. PACS are governed by the Cooperative Acts of their respective states and guided by State Bye-laws. They engage directly with rural (agricultural) borrowers, extending loans, overseeing loan repayments, and managing marketing and distribution functions. Notably, the National Cooperative Database (NCD) portal records the presence of 1,03,304 PACS in the country, with around 95% (i.e., 98,486) of them are being functional in rural areas. Significantly, the growth of PACS has been substantial, expanding from approximately 2,982 PACS in 1900-1923 to 14,391 PACS in 2011-2023. Maharashtra has the highest number of PACS (21,059) followed by Gujarat (10,266) and Bihar (8,476). Kerala boasts the highest number of members (2,56,28,261), trailed by Bihar (1,36,29,113) and Tamil Nadu (1,33,39,395). Around 78% PACS (78,489) are affiliated with Federations/ Unions. Out of total 2,69,503 gram panchayats, around 89% (i.e., 2,41,075) panchayats are covered under PACS. Importantly, strengthening PACS involves enhancing their capacity and effectiveness to provide a spectrum of services to farmers and rural communities beyond credit and financial services. Governments and stakeholders aim to uplift rural communities, improve the overall state of agriculture, and foster inclusive economic growth by reinforcing PACS. These efforts will contribute towards reducing poverty, ensuring food security, and promoting sustainable development in agrarian economies. A1. top3.text: 3 PACS Computerisation Project - Guidelines 1 Introduction The Primary Agriculture Credit Societies (PACS) form the vital third tier in the three- tier structure of the Short Term Cooperative Credit Structure (STCCS). The other two tiers are comprised of District Central Cooperative Bank (DCCBs) (2nd tier) and State Cooperative Bank (StCBs) (1st tier). National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development (NABARD), has earlier taken the initiative to bring most of the StCBs and DCCBs on Core Banking Solutions (CBS) platform which has enabled them to give modern-day technology-based banking facilities to their clients. However, the PACS have so far been largely out of the ambit of the technology support. PACS are owned by farmers, rural artisans etc. and aim at promoting thrift and mutual help among the members; cater to their credit requirements and provide credit-linked services like input supply, storage and marketing of agricultural produce etc. DCCBs provide direct linkages to the PACS through direct financing. The StCBs are primarily responsible for control and coordination of the finances of DCCBs. The large out-reach of PACS to the Small and Marginal Farmers (SMFs) make them a systemically important class of agricultural credit purveying institutions. Further, there is a felt need to develop cooperatives as vibrant business enterprises by enabling them to provide multiple services to their members with support of technology in order to fulfil members’ requirements. Keeping in view the above and to make PACS self-reliant in tune with ‘Atmanirbhar Bharat Abhiyaan’, the Government of India (GoI) has, on 29th June 2022 approved the Centrally Sponsored Project for Computerisation of Primary Agricultural Credit Societies for a period of five years from 2022-23 to 2026-27. 2 Aims & Objectives of the Project The aims and objectives of the project inter alia include the following: a. 49 Sector-wise Cooperatives L ong-term rural credit cooperatives were established for providing funds for investment in agriculture – including land development, farm mechanisation and minor irrigation - rural industries and housing. This structure consists of 14 State Cooperative Agriculture and Rural Development Banks (SCARDBs) operating at the state level and 533 Primary Cooperative Agriculture and Rural Development Banks (PCARDBs) operating at the district/ block level. The structure of long-term rural credit cooperatives differs across states. States like Jammu and Kashmir, Tripura, Uttar Pradesh, Gujarat and Puducherry follow a unitary structure i.e., SCARDBs operate through their own branches with no separate PCARDBs. On the other hand, states like Haryana, Punjab, Rajasthan, Karnataka, Kerala, and Tamil Nadu follow a federal structure wherein SCARDBs lend through PCARDBs. In two states viz., Himachal Pradesh and West Bengal, SCARDBs operate through PCARDBs as well as through their own branches. The business model of SCARDBs and PCARDBs depends heavily on borrowings; the former borrow from institutions such as NABARD for direct lending as well as lending through PCARDBs. The financial health of PCARDBs is, however, more fragile than SCARDBs, given the high share of accumulated losses on their balance sheets. A2.
