In last two years, since the formation of Ministry of Cooperation, the cooperative movement has been strengthened due to several path-breaking initiatives of the Ministry. One of the initiatives is creation of National Cooperative Database in coordination with States/UTs Government. The comprehensive national database will comprise data of various kinds of cooperatives–from the lowest unit of the cooperative sector, that is, Primary Agricultural Credit Societies (PACS) to national-level institutions. By systematically verifying the grassroots presence of cooperatives, this sector is becoming more streamlined and effective in its operations. This revolutionary initiative not only facilitates the identification of active cooperative societies, but also assists the Government in the formulation of policies to strengthen the cooperative sector to elevate the standard of living for the underprivileged and marginalized sections of society. 2.2 Need for Database Despite India being home to almost 25% of total cooperative societies in the world and with history of cooperative movement in India dating back to more than a century, there was no comprehensive, authentic and updated data repository in the country about cooperatives, their activities, their members, their financial details etc. The availability of organized database of the cooperatives, can help in formulating programs and schemes, mentioning the exact number of beneficiaries. The Ministry of Cooperation was constituted on 6th July, 2021 with a mandate, inter alia to strengthen cooperative movement in the country and deepening its reach up to grassroots; and creation of appropriate policy, legal and institutional framework to help cooperatives realize their potential. To fulfil this mandate, the process for developing a National Cooperative Database was initiated by the Ministry in consultation with the State/UT Governments, National Cooperative Federations, Central line Ministries and all other Stakeholders at various levels. 2.3 Scope & Benefits of National Cooperative Database The objective of developing National Cooperative Database (NCD) is to provide: • A single point access to authentic and updated information on cooperatives of different sectors and develop a process for better understanding of cooperatives. • The database will function as the main planning tool for Central Ministries, State Governments, Cooperative Federations, Cooperators and Sectoral Institutions like NABARD, etc., for cooperative sector. • The database would also bring synergy among various databases maintained by Central line Ministries and State Governments. • It would also help in identifying gaps/ vacuums in geographical distribution of cooperatives in the country and establishing upward/downward linkages of cooperative societies (Primary to Apex). The National Cooperative Database (NCD) captures data on several parameters related to cooperatives i.e., location details, number of members, economic activities, their upward and downward linkages, level of operations, assets and liabilities, etc. It involved development of a web based secure system to facilitate data feeding from each of the district registrar/functional registrar office which can be viewed and verified by respective state registrar office. 52 National Cooperative Database 2023 : A Report C redit and Thrift Societies are member-driven financial institutions registered under the Cooperative Societies Act of various states in India. They play a very significant role in meeting credit needs of poor and marginalized sections of the society. They offer customized loan products and repayment schedules based on members’ needs and income levels and foster a sense of community and social responsibility among members. In India, there are 79,795 primary credit and thrift societies in 34 States, except for Ladakh and Kerala, with 4.32 crore members. Out of 79,795 societies, 66,713 societies are functional, 10,489 are dormant and 2,593 are under liquidation. Around 56% societies i.e., 44,404 are operating in urban areas and the remaining 35,391 societies are operating in rural areas. Telangana and Maharashtra have the maximum number of credit and thrift societies. Approximately 55% of the total primary credit and thrift societies are operating in these two states alone. The remaining 45% of the societies are operating in 32 states. Telangana state has the highest number of societies i.e., 24,020 with a membership base of 47.77 lakh followed by Maharashtra which has 20,337 societies with 2.27 crore members. The core functions of these societies are: • Thrift: Encouraging members to save regularly through deposits, often with attractive interest rates compared to traditional savings accounts. • Credit: Providing loans to members for various purposes like education, medical expenses, business ventures, or agricultural needs, often at lower interest rates than commercial banks. • Other Services: Many societies offer additional services like micro-insurance, money transfers, and financial literacy programs. 35 Sector-wise Cooperatives Collectives, including cooperatives, mandate their members to pool in surplus money for onward lending to borrower members. Some of these adhere to the principle of self-help where the products and services are used entirely by their members. Emerging collectives, including credit cooperatives, carry out bulk of their business with non-members. Credit Cooperatives – both banks and credit societies–are the lifeline for all economic activities of members. A strong urban and rural cooperative banking and credit sector can play a catalytic role for growth of cooperatives in various segments of economy. Cooperative banks are basically cooperative societies which are registered under the Cooperative Societies Act of the State concerned or under the Multi-State Cooperative Societies (Amendment) Act, 2023. While cooperative societies functioning within a single state are governed by Cooperative Societies Act of their respective state, cooperative societies functioning in more than one State/ UT are governed by Multi-State Cooperative Societies (Amendment) Act, 2023 under the purview of Government of India. When cooperative societies carry on the business of banking, they come under the regulatory purview of RBI and they are licensed under the provisions of the Banking Regulation Act. The cooperative banking structure in India was developed to complement and supplement the commercial banking structure, with a specific focus on serving the requirements of marginalised borrowers and meeting the development needs of rural as well as urban areas. Urban Cooperative Banks (UCBs) are classified as scheduled and non-scheduled, based on their inclusion or otherwise in the second schedule of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934, and their geographical outreach (single-state or multi-state). Rural cooperatives are segregated by their lending activity, i.e., into short-term vis-à-vis long-term lending. Rural credit short-term credits are channelled through StCB, DCCBs and PACS. Rural long-term credits are disbursed through SCARDBs and PCARDBs. A. Credit Sector Sector-wise Cooperatives

49 Sector-wise Cooperatives L ong-term rural credit cooperatives were established for providing funds for investment in agriculture – including land development, farm mechanisation and minor irrigation - rural industries and housing. This structure consists of 14 State Cooperative Agriculture and Rural Development Banks (SCARDBs) operating at the state level and 533 Primary Cooperative Agriculture and Rural Development Banks (PCARDBs) operating at the district/ block level. The structure of long-term rural credit cooperatives differs across states. States like Jammu and Kashmir, Tripura, Uttar Pradesh, Gujarat and Puducherry follow a unitary structure i.e., SCARDBs operate through their own branches with no separate PCARDBs. On the other hand, states like Haryana, Punjab, Rajasthan, Karnataka, Kerala, and Tamil Nadu follow a federal structure wherein SCARDBs lend through PCARDBs. In two states viz., Himachal Pradesh and West Bengal, SCARDBs operate through PCARDBs as well as through their own branches. The business model of SCARDBs and PCARDBs depends heavily on borrowings; the former borrow from institutions such as NABARD for direct lending as well as lending through PCARDBs. The financial health of PCARDBs is, however, more fragile than SCARDBs, given the high share of accumulated losses on their balance sheets. A2. 36 National Cooperative Database 2023 : A Report P rimary Agriculture Credit Societies (PACS) constitute the lowest tier of the Short-Term Cooperative Credit Structure (STCCS) in the country, primarily providing short-term and medium-term credit facility and other input services, like seed, fertilizer, pesticide distribution, etc. to member farmers. PACS are refinanced by NABARD through District Central Cooperative Banks (DCCBs) and State Cooperative Banks (StCBs). Being the grassroots level cooperative institutions, PACS play a crucial role in sustaining the rural economy of the country by purveying institutional credit to small and marginal farmers. PACS are governed by the Cooperative Acts of their respective states and guided by State Bye-laws. They engage directly with rural (agricultural) borrowers, extending loans, overseeing loan repayments, and managing marketing and distribution functions. Notably, the National Cooperative Database (NCD) portal records the presence of 1,03,304 PACS in the country, with around 95% (i.e., 98,486) of them are being functional in rural areas. Significantly, the growth of PACS has been substantial, expanding from approximately 2,982 PACS in 1900-1923 to 14,391 PACS in 2011-2023. Maharashtra has the highest number of PACS (21,059) followed by Gujarat (10,266) and Bihar (8,476). Kerala boasts the highest number of members (2,56,28,261), trailed by Bihar (1,36,29,113) and Tamil Nadu (1,33,39,395). Around 78% PACS (78,489) are affiliated with Federations/ Unions. Out of total 2,69,503 gram panchayats, around 89% (i.e., 2,41,075) panchayats are covered under PACS. Importantly, strengthening PACS involves enhancing their capacity and effectiveness to provide a spectrum of services to farmers and rural communities beyond credit and financial services. Governments and stakeholders aim to uplift rural communities, improve the overall state of agriculture, and foster inclusive economic growth by reinforcing PACS. These efforts will contribute towards reducing poverty, ensuring food security, and promoting sustainable development in agrarian economies. A1. मतिान करने की अनुमजत िी िाएगी । ऐसी ििा में भुगतान की गई आपजत्त फीस िब् त कर ली िाएगी । (10) मतिान के अंत में ररटर्नंग अजधकारी एकजत्रत आपजत्त फीस, आपजत्त करने वाले ्‍ यजियों को वापस की गई फीस और िब् त की गई फीस का जहसाब तैयार करेगा और साथ में प्रत् येक मामले में संजिप् त िांच के पश् चातम उसके द्वारा जलए गए जनणायों का संजिप् त सार सोसाइटी को िेगा । (11) यदि मतिान के दकसी चरण में, िंगा या हंगामा द्वारा कायावाही अवरुद्ध या बाजधत होती है या यदि ऐसे जनवााचन में दकसी पयााप् त कारणों से मतिान कराना संभव नहीं है तो ररटर्नंग अजधकारी को मतिान रे करने के ऐसे कारणों को अजभलेजखत करने के पश् चातम, मतिान रे करने की िजि होगी । (12) मतिान के जलए जनयत समय के पश् चातम दकसी मतिाता को मतिान करने की अनुमजत नहीं िी िाएगी । परंतु दक यदि कोई मतिाता, मतिान के समय की समाजप्त के पूवा पररसर में प्रवेि कर चुका हो तो उसे मतपत्र िारी कर मतिान करने की अनुमजत िी िाएगी । (13) मतिान की समाजप्त के ीक पश् चातम मतगणना आरंभ की िाएगी और यदि ररटर्नंग अजधकारी के जनयंत्रण से परे यदि मतों की गणना तुरंत संभव नहीं है तो मतपेटी को ररटर्नंग अजधकारी और जनवााचन में खड़े अभ् यर्थायों या उनके एिेंटों के मुहरों से मुहरबंि कर दिया िाएगा, और यदि यह उनकी इच् छा हो तो मतपेरटयां सोसाइटी की सुरजित अजभरिा में िमा कर िी िाएगी और ऐसी जस्ट्थजत में ररटर्नंग अजधकारी अगले दिन आरंभ होने वाली मतगणना का स्ट् थान और समय की घोिणा करेगा और अभ् यथी और उसके अजभकतााओं को जलजखत में भी सूजचत करेगा और मतगणना अगले दिन ररटर्नंग अजधकारी द्वारा या उसके पयावेिण में की िाएगी और प्रत् येक अभ् यथी और उनके प्राजधकृत अजभकताा को मतगणना के समय उपजस्ट्थत रहने का अजधकार होगा तथा दकसी अभ् यथी या उसके अजभकताा के मतगणना में अनुपजस्ट्थत रहने से ररटर्नंग अजधकारी द्वारा मतगणना या पररणाम की घोिणा जनष् प्रभावी नहीं होगी । (14) ररटर्नंग अजधकारी द्वारा मतगणना की समाजप्त के पश् चातम, वह मतिान के पररणाम की एक जववरणी तैयार करेगा और प्राजधकरण के पूवाानुमोिन से तुरंत पररणाम घोजित करेगा ।

प्रस्ट् तुत करने के जलए, िो िांच अजधकारी की राय में िांच की जवियवस्ट् तु के जलए उपयोगी या संब ंजधत हो सकेगा, समन िेकर उसकी उपजस्ट्थजत सुजनजश्चत करने की िजि होगी और यदि कोई ्‍ यजि िांच अजधकारी के समि उपजस्ट्थत होने की अपेिा में असफल, उपेिा या इंकार करता है, तो िांच अजधकारी ऐसे ्‍ यजि की अनुपजस्ट्थजत में, कारणों को अजभजलजखत करने के पश् चातम िांच की कारावाई कर सकता है । (6) नोरटस िारी होने की तारीख से छह महीनों की अवजध के भीतर िांच अजधकारी द्वारा िांच पूरी की िाएगी और िांच में जनष् किों की ररपोटा केन्द् रीय सरकार को प्रस्ट् तुत की िाएगी । 19ङ. प्राजधकरण की बै कें- (1) प्राजधकरण अपने कारबार के संबंध में, िब कभी आवश् यक हो, बै क करेगा । (2) प्राजधकरण, बैं कों के आयोिन की अपनी प्रदक्रया और अपने मध् य काया का जवतरण स्ट् वयं जनधााररत करेगा । (3) प्राजधकरण की बै क की गणपूर्ता, सभापजत और उप-सभापजत सजहत तीन सिस्ट् यों से कम की नहीं होगी । (4) ररजि की ििा में,केन्द् रीय सरकार के अनुमोिन से गणपूर्ता को अनुपाजतक ूपप से घटाया िा सकता है । 19च. सहकारी जनवााचन प्राजधकरण की िजियां और कृत् य - सहकारी सोसाइरटयों का जनवााचन कराने के जलए प्राजधकरण की जनम् नजलजखत िजियां होंगी, अथाातम:— (क) प्राजधकरण जनवााचन कराने के प्रयोिन से, दकसी बहुराज् य सहकारी सोसाइटी, राज् य सरकार, या केन्द् रीय सरकार के दकसी अजधकारी या, सेवारत या सेवाजनवृत्त कमाचारी सजहत, िो दकसी पि पर या ऐसे पिनाम और कत्ता्‍ यों के साथ इस उेेश् य से तैयार पैनल में से पयावेिकों, ररटर्नंग अजधकाररयों और सहायक ररटर्नंग अजधकाररयों सजहत दकसी ्‍ यजि को जनयुि करना:

पश् चातम, प्रत् येक अभ् यथी द्वारा प्राप् त मतों की संख् या और जनवााचन के पररणाम की घोिणा करेगा । (5) ररटर्नंग अजधकारी इसके ीक पश् चातम पिाजधकाररयों के जनवााचन की कायावाजहयों को एक ररपोटा में अजभलेजखत करेगा िो सोसाइटी के अजभलेख का एक भाग होगा और सभी पर बाध् यकारी होगा । ररटर्नंग अजधकारी ऐसी ररपोटा की एक प्रजतजलजप के साथ मतिान की जववरणी की एक प्रजतजलजप प्राजधकरण को सौंपेगा। (6) ररटर्नंग अजधकारी द्वारा जनवााचन के पररणाम की घोिणा प्राजधकरण के पूवा अनुमोिन से करेगा। (7) ररटर्नंग अजधकारी द्वारा पररणामों की घोिण के पश् चातम, बहुराज् य सहकारी सोसाइटी के मुख् य कायाकारी द्वारा जनवााचन प्रमाणपत्र तुरंत िारी दकए िाएंगे। 19-ण. मतगणना के जलए जनयत स्ट् थान पर प्रवेि - (1) ररटर्नंग अजधकारी, मतगणना के जलए जनयत स्ट् थान से जनम् नजलजखत के जसवाए, सभी ्‍ यजियों को बाहर रखेगा,— (क) ऐसे ्‍ यजियों को जिन्द् हें वह गणना में सहायता हेतु जनयुक्ट् त करे; (ख) ररटर्नंग अजधकारी द्वारा प्राजधकृत ्‍ यजि; (ग) जनवााचन से संबंजधत ड्यूटी पर लोक सेवक; और (घ) अभ् यथी । (2) ऐसे दकसी ्‍ यजि को िो जनवााचन में दकसी अभ् यथी के जलए अन्द् यथा काया कर रहा हो, उपजनयम (1) के खंड (क) के अधीन जनयुक्ट् त नहीं दकया िाएगा । (3) कोई ्‍ यजि िो मतगणना के िौरान किाचार करता है या ररटर्नंग अजधकारी के जवजधक जनिेिों का पालन करने में जवफल रहता है तो उसे मतगणना स्ट् थल से ररटर्नंग अजधकारी द्वारा या जनवााचन ड्यूटी पर तैनात दकसी पुजलस कमी द्वारा या इस जनजमत्त ररटर्नंग अजधकारी द्वारा प्राजधकृत दकए गए दकसी ्‍ यजि द्वारा हटा दिया िाएगा ।

य सहकारी सोसाइटी का मुख् य कायाकारी ऐसी ररजियों की सूचना, इसके उद्भुत होने के एक सप् ताह के भीतर प्राजधकरण को संसूजचत करेगा, िो अजधजनयम की धारा 45ञ के उपबंधों के अनुसार ररजियों को भरने की कारावाई करेगा । (2) अजधजनयम की धारा 45ञ के उपबंधों के अनुसार वैकजल्पक ररजियों में जनयुक्ट् त कोई ्‍ यजि अजधिेि अवजध तक ही बोडा का सिस्ट् य रहेगा, िब तक वह बोडा के सिस्ट् य जिसके स्ट् थान पर जनयुक्ट् त हुआ है, रहेगा । 19य. मतिान की गोपनीयता का अनुरिण - प्रत् येक अजधकारी, जलजपक, अजभकताा या अन्द् य ्‍ यजि िो दकसी जनवााचन में अजभलेखन या मतगणना से िुड़ा काया जनष् पािन कर रहा है, मतगणना की गोपनीयता अनुरजित करेगा और अनुरिण करने में मिि करेगा और दकसी अन्द् य ्‍ यजि को (जसवाए कुछ प्रयोिनों के जलए दकसी जवजध द्वारा या उसके अधीन प्राजधकृत) ऐसी गोपनीयता का उल् लंघन करने के जलए मतिान से संबंजधत कोई सूचना संप्रेजित नहीं करेगा ।” 5. मूल जनयमों में, जनयम 20 के स्ट् थान पर जनम् नजलजखत जनयम रखे िाएंगे, अथाातम: -

ही जछदरत अधपन्द् ने पर उक्ट् त सिस्ट् य या प्रजतजनजध का हस्ट् तािर या अंगु े की छाप लेकर उसे मत पत्र िारी करेगा और अधपन्द् ने पर मतपत्र का क्रमांक और अन्द् य जववरण होगा तथा मतपत्र प्राप् त करने के बाि, सिस्ट् य पृथक स्ट् थाजपत मतिान कंपाटामेंट िाएगा और पूरी गोपनीयता के साथ अभ् यथी या अभ् यर्थायों, िो भी ििा हो, के नाम के आगे जिसे वह अपना मत िेना चाहता है, ‘X’ का जचह्न लगाकर अपने मताजधकार का प्रयोग करके मतपत्र को इस प्रयोिन हेतु रखी मतपेटी में डालेगा । परंतु दक िृजिहीनता या अन्द् य िारीररक दि्‍ यांगता या जनरिरता के कारण यदि कोई सिस्ट् य मतपत्र पर जनिान लगाने में असमथा है तो मतिान अजधकारी, और िहां ऐसे मतिान अजधकारी जनयुक्ट् त नहीं हैं, वहां ररटर्नंग अजधकारी उससे अभ् यथी या अभ् यर्थायों का नाम सुजनजश्चत करेगा जिसके पि में वह अपना मत िेने को इच् छुक है और उसकी ओर से ‘X’ का जनिान लगाकर मतपत्र को मतपेटी में डालेगा । (8) प्रत् येक सिस्ट् य जिसका नाम मतिान के जलए पात्र सिस्ट् यों/प्रजतजनजधयों की सूची में प्रजवष् ट है, जिसे मतिान अजधकारी को सुपुिा दकया गया है, को अपना मतिान करने का हक है िबतक दक उसकी पहचान के जवरुद्ध अभ् यथी या उसके अजभकताा द्वारा आपजत्त न हो । यदि दकसी सिस्ट् य के जवरुद्ध ऐसी कोई आपजत्त आती है या यदि मतिान अजधकारी को कोई तकासंगत संिेह को, तो वह मामले को ररटर्नंग अजधकारी को संिर्भात करेगा िो एक संजिप् त िांच करके सोसाइटी के ररकॉडा के संिभा में आपजत्त पर जनणाय करेगा । (9) ररटर्नंग अजधकारी दकसी अभ् यथी या उसके मतिान अजभकताा द्वारा दकसी सिस्ट् य की पहचान से संबंजधत दकसी आपजत्त पर तब तक जवचार नहीं करेगा िब तक दक आपजत्त करने वाले ्‍ यजि ने प्रत् येक ऐसे मत के जलए 5/- रुपए की फीस का संिाय न कर दिया हो और ररटर्नंग अजधकारी तत् पश् चातम आपजत्त पर जवचार करेगा और मतिान करने आए सिस्ट् य से उसके अंगु े की छाप या हस्ट् तािर, िो भी ििा हो, उसकी पहचान का वणान करने वाली उघोषोिणा पर लेगा और यदि वह ऐसा करने से इंकार करता है तो उसे मतिान करने की अनुमजत नहीं िी िाएगी और यदि िूसरी ओर, ऐसी संजिप् त छानबीन पर ररटर्नंग अजधकारी की संतुजि के अनुसार सिस्ट् य की पहचान स्ट् थाजपत हो िाती है तो मतिान अजधकारी मतपत्र िारी करेगा और सिस्ट् य को तब मतिान करने की अनुमजत िी िाएगी Primary Agricultural Credit Societies (PACS) are village- or panchayat-level cooperative societies that form the lowest tier of the Short-Term Cooperative Credit Structure. PACS deal directly with rural and agricultural borrowers. They provide loans, collect repayment of loans, and may undertake distribution and marketing functions. PACS are an important link between farmers and the higher levels of the cooperative credit system, including District Central Cooperative Banks (DCCBs), State Cooperative Banks (StCBs), and NABARD. --- ## Why are PACS Important? PACS help connect farmers and rural communities with: * Agricultural credit * Farm inputs * Agricultural services * Storage facilities * Markets and distribution * Other cooperative and government-supported services The Ministry of Cooperation describes PACS as the grassroots base of the cooperative credit structure. PACS can help bring farmers closer to credit, agricultural inputs, markets and value addition. --- ## What Services Can PACS Provide? Traditional PACS activities include: * Short-term agricultural credit * Medium-term credit * Distribution of seeds * Distribution of fertilizers * Distribution of pesticides * Storage-related services * Agricultural input services * Marketing and distribution functions * Loan repayment and related credit services Under the Model Bye-laws and diversification initiatives, PACS can also undertake multiple activities beyond traditional credit. These may include: * Dairy activities * Fisheries activities * Floriculture * Food-grain procurement * Warehousing and storage * Fair Price Shops * LPG/CNG/Petrol/Diesel distributorship * Common Service Centre (CSC) services * Business Correspondent or banking-related activities * Insurance-related services * Custom Hiring Centres * Other permitted business activities The exact activities available at an individual PACS depend on its applicable State Cooperative Societies Act, bye-laws, permissions and local implementation. --- ## What Types of Loans Does PACS Provide? PACS traditionally provide: * Short-term agricultural credit * Medium-term agricultural credit The Model Bye-laws and computerization framework also cover financial services involving short-, medium- and long-term loans. However, the exact loan products, limits, interest rates, repayment periods and eligibility conditions depend on the applicable cooperative rules, State provisions and the individual PACS or financing structure. Primary Agricultural Credit Societies (PACS) are village- or panchayat-level cooperative societies that form the lowest tier of the Short-Term Cooperative Credit Structure. PACS deal directly with rural and agricultural borrowers. They provide loans, collect repayment of loans, and may undertake distribution and marketing functions. PACS are an important link between farmers and the higher levels of the cooperative credit system, including District Central Cooperative Banks (DCCBs), State Cooperative Banks (StCBs), and NABARD. --- ## Why are PACS Important? PACS help connect farmers and rural communities with: * Agricultural credit * Farm inputs * Agricultural services * Storage facilities * Markets and distribution * Other cooperative and government-supported services The Ministry of Cooperation describes PACS as the grassroots base of the cooperative credit structure. PACS can help bring farmers closer to credit, agricultural inputs, markets and value addition. --- ## What Services Can PACS Provide? Traditional PACS activities include: * Short-term agricultural credit * Medium-term credit * Distribution of seeds * Distribution of fertilizers * Distribution of pesticides * Storage-related services * Agricultural input services * Marketing and distribution functions * Loan repayment and related credit services Under the Model Bye-laws and diversification initiatives, PACS can also undertake multiple activities beyond traditional credit. These may include: * Dairy activities * Fisheries activities * Floriculture * Food-grain procurement * Warehousing and storage * Fair Price Shops * LPG/CNG/Petrol/Diesel distributorship * Common Service Centre (CSC) services * Business Correspondent or banking-related activities * Insurance-related services * Custom Hiring Centres * Other permitted business activities The exact activities available at an individual PACS depend on its applicable State Cooperative Societies Act, bye-laws, permissions and local implementation. --- ## What Types of Loans Does PACS Provide? PACS traditionally provide: * Short-term agricultural credit * Medium-term agricultural credit The Model Bye-laws and computerization framework also cover financial services involving short-, medium- and long-term loans. However, the exact loan products, limits, interest rates, repayment periods and eligibility conditions depend on the applicable cooperative rules, State provisions and the individual PACS or financing structure. 36 National Cooperative Database 2023 : A Report P rimary Agriculture Credit Societies (PACS) constitute the lowest tier of the Short-Term Cooperative Credit Structure (STCCS) in the country, primarily providing short-term and medium-term credit facility and other input services, like seed, fertilizer, pesticide distribution, etc. to member farmers. PACS are refinanced by NABARD through District Central Cooperative Banks (DCCBs) and State Cooperative Banks (StCBs). Being the grassroots level cooperative institutions, PACS play a crucial role in sustaining the rural economy of the country by purveying institutional credit to small and marginal farmers. PACS are governed by the Cooperative Acts of their respective states and guided by State Bye-laws. They engage directly with rural (agricultural) borrowers, extending loans, overseeing loan repayments, and managing marketing and distribution functions. Notably, the National Cooperative Database (NCD) portal records the presence of 1,03,304 PACS in the country, with around 95% (i.e., 98,486) of them are being functional in rural areas. Significantly, the growth of PACS has been substantial, expanding from approximately 2,982 PACS in 1900-1923 to 14,391 PACS in 2011-2023. Maharashtra has the highest number of PACS (21,059) followed by Gujarat (10,266) and Bihar (8,476). Kerala boasts the highest number of members (2,56,28,261), trailed by Bihar (1,36,29,113) and Tamil Nadu (1,33,39,395). Around 78% PACS (78,489) are affiliated with Federations/ Unions. Out of total 2,69,503 gram panchayats, around 89% (i.e., 2,41,075) panchayats are covered under PACS. Importantly, strengthening PACS involves enhancing their capacity and effectiveness to provide a spectrum of services to farmers and rural communities beyond credit and financial services. Governments and stakeholders aim to uplift rural communities, improve the overall state of agriculture, and foster inclusive economic growth by reinforcing PACS. These efforts will contribute towards reducing poverty, ensuring food security, and promoting sustainable development in agrarian economies. A1. top3.text: 3 PACS Computerisation Project - Guidelines 1 Introduction The Primary Agriculture Credit Societies (PACS) form the vital third tier in the three- tier structure of the Short Term Cooperative Credit Structure (STCCS). The other two tiers are comprised of District Central Cooperative Bank (DCCBs) (2nd tier) and State Cooperative Bank (StCBs) (1st tier). National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development (NABARD), has earlier taken the initiative to bring most of the StCBs and DCCBs on Core Banking Solutions (CBS) platform which has enabled them to give modern-day technology-based banking facilities to their clients. However, the PACS have so far been largely out of the ambit of the technology support. PACS are owned by farmers, rural artisans etc. and aim at promoting thrift and mutual help among the members; cater to their credit requirements and provide credit-linked services like input supply, storage and marketing of agricultural produce etc. DCCBs provide direct linkages to the PACS through direct financing. The StCBs are primarily responsible for control and coordination of the finances of DCCBs. The large out-reach of PACS to the Small and Marginal Farmers (SMFs) make them a systemically important class of agricultural credit purveying institutions. Further, there is a felt need to develop cooperatives as vibrant business enterprises by enabling them to provide multiple services to their members with support of technology in order to fulfil members’ requirements. This structure consists of 14 State Cooperative Agriculture and Rural Development Banks (SCARDBs) operating at the state level and 533 Primary Cooperative Agriculture and Rural Development Banks (PCARDBs) operating at the district/ block level. The structure of long-term rural credit cooperatives differs across states. States like Jammu and Kashmir, Tripura, Uttar Pradesh, Gujarat and Puducherry follow a unitary structure i.e., SCARDBs operate through their own branches with no separate PCARDBs. On the other hand, states like Haryana, Punjab, Rajasthan, Karnataka, Kerala, and Tamil Nadu follow a federal structure wherein SCARDBs lend through PCARDBs. In two states viz., Himachal Pradesh and West Bengal, SCARDBs operate through PCARDBs as well as through their own branches. The business model of SCARDBs and PCARDBs depends heavily on borrowings; the former borrow from institutions such as NABARD for direct lending as well as lending through PCARDBs. The financial health of PCARDBs is, however, more fragile than SCARDBs, given the high share of accumulated losses on their balance sheets. A2. 35 Sector-wise Cooperatives Collectives, including cooperatives, mandate their members to pool in surplus money for onward lending to borrower members. Some of these adhere to the principle of self-help where the products and services are used entirely by their members. Emerging collectives, including credit cooperatives, carry out bulk of their business with non-members. Credit Cooperatives – both banks and credit societies–are the lifeline for all economic activities of members. A strong urban and rural cooperative banking and credit sector can play a catalytic role for growth of cooperatives in various segments of economy. Cooperative banks are basically cooperative societies which are registered under the Cooperative Societies Act of the State concerned or under the Multi-State Cooperative Societies (Amendment) Act, 2023. While cooperative societies functioning within a single state are governed by Cooperative Societies Act of their respective state, cooperative societies functioning in more than one State/ UT are governed by Multi-State Cooperative Societies (Amendment) Act, 2023 under the purview of Government of India. When cooperative societies carry on the business of banking, they come under the regulatory purview of RBI and they are licensed under the provisions of the Banking Regulation Act. The cooperative banking structure in India was developed to complement and supplement the commercial banking structure, with a specific focus on serving the requirements of marginalised borrowers and meeting the development needs of rural as well as urban areas. Urban Cooperative Banks (UCBs) are classified as scheduled and non-scheduled, based on their inclusion or otherwise in the second schedule of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934, and their geographical outreach (single-state or multi-state). Rural cooperatives are segregated by their lending activity, i.e., into short-term vis-à-vis long-term lending. Rural credit short-term credits are channelled through StCB, DCCBs and PACS. Rural long-term credits are disbursed through SCARDBs and PCARDBs. A. Credit Sector Sector-wise Cooperatives

In last two years, since the formation of Ministry of Cooperation, the cooperative movement has been strengthened due to several path-breaking initiatives of the Ministry. One of the initiatives is creation of National Cooperative Database in coordination with States/UTs Government. The comprehensive national database will comprise data of various kinds of cooperatives–from the lowest unit of the cooperative sector, that is, Primary Agricultural Credit Societies (PACS) to national-level institutions. By systematically verifying the grassroots presence of cooperatives, this sector is becoming more streamlined and effective in its operations. This revolutionary initiative not only facilitates the identification of active cooperative societies, but also assists the Government in the formulation of policies to strengthen the cooperative sector to elevate the standard of living for the underprivileged and marginalized sections of society. 2.2 Need for Database Despite India being home to almost 25% of total cooperative societies in the world and with history of cooperative movement in India dating back to more than a century, there was no comprehensive, authentic and updated data repository in the country about cooperatives, their activities, their members, their financial details etc. The availability of organized database of the cooperatives, can help in formulating programs and schemes, mentioning the exact number of beneficiaries. The Ministry of Cooperation was constituted on 6th July, 2021 with a mandate, inter alia to strengthen cooperative movement in the country and deepening its reach up to grassroots; and creation of appropriate policy, legal and institutional framework to help cooperatives realize their potential. To fulfil this mandate, the process for developing a National Cooperative Database was initiated by the Ministry in consultation with the State/UT Governments, National Cooperative Federations, Central line Ministries and all other Stakeholders at various levels. 2.3 Scope & Benefits of National Cooperative Database The objective of developing National Cooperative Database (NCD) is to provide: • A single point access to authentic and updated information on cooperatives of different sectors and develop a process for better understanding of cooperatives. • The database will function as the main planning tool for Central Ministries, State Governments, Cooperative Federations, Cooperators and Sectoral Institutions like NABARD, etc., for cooperative sector. • The database would also bring synergy among various databases maintained by Central line Ministries and State Governments. • It would also help in identifying gaps/ vacuums in geographical distribution of cooperatives in the country and establishing upward/downward linkages of cooperative societies (Primary to Apex). 36 National Cooperative Database 2023 : A Report P rimary Agriculture Credit Societies (PACS) constitute the lowest tier of the Short-Term Cooperative Credit Structure (STCCS) in the country, primarily providing short-term and medium-term credit facility and other input services, like seed, fertilizer, pesticide distribution, etc. to member farmers. PACS are refinanced by NABARD through District Central Cooperative Banks (DCCBs) and State Cooperative Banks (StCBs). Being the grassroots level cooperative institutions, PACS play a crucial role in sustaining the rural economy of the country by purveying institutional credit to small and marginal farmers. PACS are governed by the Cooperative Acts of their respective states and guided by State Bye-laws. They engage directly with rural (agricultural) borrowers, extending loans, overseeing loan repayments, and managing marketing and distribution functions. Notably, the National Cooperative Database (NCD) portal records the presence of 1,03,304 PACS in the country, with around 95% (i.e., 98,486) of them are being functional in rural areas. Significantly, the growth of PACS has been substantial, expanding from approximately 2,982 PACS in 1900-1923 to 14,391 PACS in 2011-2023. Maharashtra has the highest number of PACS (21,059) followed by Gujarat (10,266) and Bihar (8,476). Kerala boasts the highest number of members (2,56,28,261), trailed by Bihar (1,36,29,113) and Tamil Nadu (1,33,39,395). Around 78% PACS (78,489) are affiliated with Federations/ Unions. Out of total 2,69,503 gram panchayats, around 89% (i.e., 2,41,075) panchayats are covered under PACS. Importantly, strengthening PACS involves enhancing their capacity and effectiveness to provide a spectrum of services to farmers and rural communities beyond credit and financial services. Governments and stakeholders aim to uplift rural communities, improve the overall state of agriculture, and foster inclusive economic growth by reinforcing PACS. These efforts will contribute towards reducing poverty, ensuring food security, and promoting sustainable development in agrarian economies. A1. top3.text: 3 PACS Computerisation Project - Guidelines 1 Introduction The Primary Agriculture Credit Societies (PACS) form the vital third tier in the three- tier structure of the Short Term Cooperative Credit Structure (STCCS). The other two tiers are comprised of District Central Cooperative Bank (DCCBs) (2nd tier) and State Cooperative Bank (StCBs) (1st tier). National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development (NABARD), has earlier taken the initiative to bring most of the StCBs and DCCBs on Core Banking Solutions (CBS) platform which has enabled them to give modern-day technology-based banking facilities to their clients. However, the PACS have so far been largely out of the ambit of the technology support. PACS are owned by farmers, rural artisans etc. and aim at promoting thrift and mutual help among the members; cater to their credit requirements and provide credit-linked services like input supply, storage and marketing of agricultural produce etc. DCCBs provide direct linkages to the PACS through direct financing. The StCBs are primarily responsible for control and coordination of the finances of DCCBs. The large out-reach of PACS to the Small and Marginal Farmers (SMFs) make them a systemically important class of agricultural credit purveying institutions. Further, there is a felt need to develop cooperatives as vibrant business enterprises by enabling them to provide multiple services to their members with support of technology in order to fulfil members’ requirements. Keeping in view the above and to make PACS self-reliant in tune with ‘Atmanirbhar Bharat Abhiyaan’, the Government of India (GoI) has, on 29th June 2022 approved the Centrally Sponsored Project for Computerisation of Primary Agricultural Credit Societies for a period of five years from 2022-23 to 2026-27. 2 Aims & Objectives of the Project The aims and objectives of the project inter alia include the following: a. To bring in efficiency, accountability, transparency at PACS and improve profitability. b. To bring in accuracy and uniformity in the conduct of business, accounting with

49 Sector-wise Cooperatives L ong-term rural credit cooperatives were established for providing funds for investment in agriculture – including land development, farm mechanisation and minor irrigation - rural industries and housing. This structure consists of 14 State Cooperative Agriculture and Rural Development Banks (SCARDBs) operating at the state level and 533 Primary Cooperative Agriculture and Rural Development Banks (PCARDBs) operating at the district/ block level. The structure of long-term rural credit cooperatives differs across states. States like Jammu and Kashmir, Tripura, Uttar Pradesh, Gujarat and Puducherry follow a unitary structure i.e., SCARDBs operate through their own branches with no separate PCARDBs. On the other hand, states like Haryana, Punjab, Rajasthan, Karnataka, Kerala, and Tamil Nadu follow a federal structure wherein SCARDBs lend through PCARDBs. In two states viz., Himachal Pradesh and West Bengal, SCARDBs operate through PCARDBs as well as through their own branches. The business model of SCARDBs and PCARDBs depends heavily on borrowings; the former borrow from institutions such as NABARD for direct lending as well as lending through PCARDBs. The financial health of PCARDBs is, however, more fragile than SCARDBs, given the high share of accumulated losses on their balance sheets. A2. State cooperative banks are the apex institutions in this structure. The National Cooperative Database (NCD) records the presence of 32 registered State Cooperative Banks in the country except for 5 States/UTs namely Haryana, Ladakh, Lakshadweep, Manipur, and Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu. These cooperative banks offer a comprehensive range of services, from savings accounts to agricultural loans, actively supporting priority sectors and contributing to the well-being of local communities. 35 Sector-wise Cooperatives Collectives, including cooperatives, mandate their members to pool in surplus money for onward lending to borrower members. Some of these adhere to the principle of self-help where the products and services are used entirely by their members. Emerging collectives, including credit cooperatives, carry out bulk of their business with non-members. Credit Cooperatives – both banks and credit societies–are the lifeline for all economic activities of members. A strong urban and rural cooperative banking and credit sector can play a catalytic role for growth of cooperatives in various segments of economy. Cooperative banks are basically cooperative societies which are registered under the Cooperative Societies Act of the State concerned or under the Multi-State Cooperative Societies (Amendment) Act, 2023. While cooperative societies functioning within a single state are governed by Cooperative Societies Act of their respective state, cooperative societies functioning in more than one State/ UT are governed by Multi-State Cooperative Societies (Amendment) Act, 2023 under the purview of Government of India. When cooperative societies carry on the business of banking, they come under the regulatory purview of RBI and they are licensed under the provisions of the Banking Regulation Act. The cooperative banking structure in India was developed to complement and supplement the commercial banking structure, with a specific focus on serving the requirements of marginalised borrowers and meeting the development needs of rural as well as urban areas. Urban Cooperative Banks (UCBs) are classified as scheduled and non-scheduled, based on their inclusion or otherwise in the second schedule of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934, and their geographical outreach (single-state or multi-state). Rural cooperatives are segregated by their lending activity, i.e., into short-term vis-à-vis long-term lending. Rural credit short-term credits are channelled through StCB, DCCBs and PACS. Rural long-term credits are disbursed through SCARDBs and PCARDBs. A. Credit Sector Sector-wise Cooperatives

In last two years, since the formation of Ministry of Cooperation, the cooperative movement has been strengthened due to several path-breaking initiatives of the Ministry. One of the initiatives is creation of National Cooperative Database in coordination with States/UTs Government. 36 National Cooperative Database 2023 : A Report P rimary Agriculture Credit Societies (PACS) constitute the lowest tier of the Short-Term Cooperative Credit Structure (STCCS) in the country, primarily providing short-term and medium-term credit facility and other input services, like seed, fertilizer, pesticide distribution, etc. to member farmers. PACS are refinanced by NABARD through District Central Cooperative Banks (DCCBs) and State Cooperative Banks (StCBs). Being the grassroots level cooperative institutions, PACS play a crucial role in sustaining the rural economy of the country by purveying institutional credit to small and marginal farmers. PACS are governed by the Cooperative Acts of their respective states and guided by State Bye-laws. They engage directly with rural (agricultural) borrowers, extending loans, overseeing loan repayments, and managing marketing and distribution functions. Notably, the National Cooperative Database (NCD) portal records the presence of 1,03,304 PACS in the country, with around 95% (i.e., 98,486) of them are being functional in rural areas. Significantly, the growth of PACS has been substantial, expanding from approximately 2,982 PACS in 1900-1923 to 14,391 PACS in 2011-2023. Maharashtra has the highest number of PACS (21,059) followed by Gujarat (10,266) and Bihar (8,476). Kerala boasts the highest number of members (2,56,28,261), trailed by Bihar (1,36,29,113) and Tamil Nadu (1,33,39,395). Around 78% PACS (78,489) are affiliated with Federations/ Unions. Out of total 2,69,503 gram panchayats, around 89% (i.e., 2,41,075) panchayats are covered under PACS. Importantly, strengthening PACS involves enhancing their capacity and effectiveness to provide a spectrum of services to farmers and rural communities beyond credit and financial services. Governments and stakeholders aim to uplift rural communities, improve the overall state of agriculture, and foster inclusive economic growth by reinforcing PACS. These efforts will contribute towards reducing poverty, ensuring food security, and promoting sustainable development in agrarian economies. A1. top3.text: 3 PACS Computerisation Project - Guidelines 1 Introduction The Primary Agriculture Credit Societies (PACS) form the vital third tier in the three- tier structure of the Short Term Cooperative Credit Structure (STCCS). The other two tiers are comprised of District Central Cooperative Bank (DCCBs) (2nd tier) and State Cooperative Bank (StCBs) (1st tier). National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development (NABARD), has earlier taken the initiative to bring most of the StCBs and DCCBs on Core Banking Solutions (CBS) platform which has enabled them to give modern-day technology-based banking facilities to their clients. However, the PACS have so far been largely out of the ambit of the technology support. PACS are owned by farmers, rural artisans etc. and aim at promoting thrift and mutual help among the members; cater to their credit requirements and provide credit-linked services like input supply, storage and marketing of agricultural produce etc. DCCBs provide direct linkages to the PACS through direct financing. The StCBs are primarily responsible for control and coordination of the finances of DCCBs. The large out-reach of PACS to the Small and Marginal Farmers (SMFs) make them a systemically important class of agricultural credit purveying institutions. Further, there is a felt need to develop cooperatives as vibrant business enterprises by enabling them to provide multiple services to their members with support of technology in order to fulfil members’ requirements. This structure consists of 14 State Cooperative Agriculture and Rural Development Banks (SCARDBs) operating at the state level and 533 Primary Cooperative Agriculture and Rural Development Banks (PCARDBs) operating at the district/ block level. The structure of long-term rural credit cooperatives differs across states. States like Jammu and Kashmir, Tripura, Uttar Pradesh, Gujarat and Puducherry follow a unitary structure i.e., SCARDBs operate through their own branches with no separate PCARDBs. On the other hand, states like Haryana, Punjab, Rajasthan, Karnataka, Kerala, and Tamil Nadu follow a federal structure wherein SCARDBs lend through PCARDBs. In two states viz., Himachal Pradesh and West Bengal, SCARDBs operate through PCARDBs as well as through their own branches. The business model of SCARDBs and PCARDBs depends heavily on borrowings; the former borrow from institutions such as NABARD for direct lending as well as lending through PCARDBs. The financial health of PCARDBs is, however, more fragile than SCARDBs, given the high share of accumulated losses on their balance sheets. A2. The National Cooperative Database (NCD) captures data on several parameters related to cooperatives i.e., location details, number of members, economic activities, their upward and downward linkages, level of operations, assets and liabilities, etc. It involved development of a web based secure system to facilitate data feeding from each of the district registrar/functional registrar office which can be viewed and verified by respective state registrar office. 35 Sector-wise Cooperatives Collectives, including cooperatives, mandate their members to pool in surplus money for onward lending to borrower members. Some of these adhere to the principle of self-help where the products and services are used entirely by their members. Emerging collectives, including credit cooperatives, carry out bulk of their business with non-members. Credit Cooperatives – both banks and credit societies–are the lifeline for all economic activities of members. A strong urban and rural cooperative banking and credit sector can play a catalytic role for growth of cooperatives in various segments of economy. Cooperative banks are basically cooperative societies which are registered under the Cooperative Societies Act of the State concerned or under the Multi-State Cooperative Societies (Amendment) Act, 2023. While cooperative societies functioning within a single state are governed by Cooperative Societies Act of their respective state, cooperative societies functioning in more than one State/ UT are governed by Multi-State Cooperative Societies (Amendment) Act, 2023 under the purview of Government of India. When cooperative societies carry on the business of banking, they come under the regulatory purview of RBI and they are licensed under the provisions of the Banking Regulation Act. The cooperative banking structure in India was developed to complement and supplement the commercial banking structure, with a specific focus on serving the requirements of marginalised borrowers and meeting the development needs of rural as well as urban areas. Urban Cooperative Banks (UCBs) are classified as scheduled and non-scheduled, based on their inclusion or otherwise in the second schedule of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934, and their geographical outreach (single-state or multi-state). Rural cooperatives are segregated by their lending activity, i.e., into short-term vis-à-vis long-term lending. Rural credit short-term credits are channelled through StCB, DCCBs and PACS. PACS deal directly with rural and agricultural borrowers. They provide loans, collect repayment of loans, and may undertake distribution and marketing functions. top3.text: 3 PACS Computerisation Project - Guidelines 1 Introduction The Primary Agriculture Credit Societies (PACS) form the vital third tier in the three- tier structure of the Short Term Cooperative Credit Structure (STCCS). The other two tiers are comprised of District Central Cooperative Bank (DCCBs) (2nd tier) and State Cooperative Bank (StCBs) (1st tier). National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development (NABARD), has earlier taken the initiative to bring most of the StCBs and DCCBs on Core Banking Solutions (CBS) platform which has enabled them to give modern-day technology-based banking facilities to their clients. However, the PACS have so far been largely out of the ambit of the technology support. PACS are owned by farmers, rural artisans etc. and aim at promoting thrift and mutual help among the members; cater to their credit requirements and provide credit-linked services like input supply, storage and marketing of agricultural produce etc. DCCBs provide direct linkages to the PACS through direct financing. The StCBs are primarily responsible for control and coordination of the finances of DCCBs. The large out-reach of PACS to the Small and Marginal Farmers (SMFs) make them a systemically important class of agricultural credit purveying institutions. Further, there is a felt need to develop cooperatives as vibrant business enterprises by enabling them to provide multiple services to their members with support of technology in order to fulfil members’ requirements. Keeping in view the above and to make PACS self-reliant in tune with ‘Atmanirbhar Bharat Abhiyaan’, the Government of India (GoI) has, on 29th June 2022 approved the Centrally Sponsored Project for Computerisation of Primary Agricultural Credit Societies for a period of five years from 2022-23 to 2026-27. 2 Aims & Objectives of the Project The aims and objectives of the project inter alia include the following: a. 36 National Cooperative Database 2023 : A Report P rimary Agriculture Credit Societies (PACS) constitute the lowest tier of the Short-Term Cooperative Credit Structure (STCCS) in the country, primarily providing short-term and medium-term credit facility and other input services, like seed, fertilizer, pesticide distribution, etc. to member farmers. PACS are refinanced by NABARD through District Central Cooperative Banks (DCCBs) and State Cooperative Banks (StCBs). Being the grassroots level cooperative institutions, PACS play a crucial role in sustaining the rural economy of the country by purveying institutional credit to small and marginal farmers. PACS are governed by the Cooperative Acts of their respective states and guided by State Bye-laws. They engage directly with rural (agricultural) borrowers, extending loans, overseeing loan repayments, and managing marketing and distribution functions. Notably, the National Cooperative Database (NCD) portal records the presence of 1,03,304 PACS in the country, with around 95% (i.e., 98,486) of them are being functional in rural areas. Significantly, the growth of PACS has been substantial, expanding from approximately 2,982 PACS in 1900-1923 to 14,391 PACS in 2011-2023. Maharashtra has the highest number of PACS (21,059) followed by Gujarat (10,266) and Bihar (8,476). Kerala boasts the highest number of members (2,56,28,261), trailed by Bihar (1,36,29,113) and Tamil Nadu (1,33,39,395). Around 78% PACS (78,489) are affiliated with Federations/ Unions. Out of total 2,69,503 gram panchayats, around 89% (i.e., 2,41,075) panchayats are covered under PACS. Importantly, strengthening PACS involves enhancing their capacity and effectiveness to provide a spectrum of services to farmers and rural communities beyond credit and financial services. Governments and stakeholders aim to uplift rural communities, improve the overall state of agriculture, and foster inclusive economic growth by reinforcing PACS. These efforts will contribute towards reducing poverty, ensuring food security, and promoting sustainable development in agrarian economies. A1. This structure consists of 14 State Cooperative Agriculture and Rural Development Banks (SCARDBs) operating at the state level and 533 Primary Cooperative Agriculture and Rural Development Banks (PCARDBs) operating at the district/ block level. The structure of long-term rural credit cooperatives differs across states. States like Jammu and Kashmir, Tripura, Uttar Pradesh, Gujarat and Puducherry follow a unitary structure i.e., SCARDBs operate through their own branches with no separate PCARDBs. On the other hand, states like Haryana, Punjab, Rajasthan, Karnataka, Kerala, and Tamil Nadu follow a federal structure wherein SCARDBs lend through PCARDBs. In two states viz., Himachal Pradesh and West Bengal, SCARDBs operate through PCARDBs as well as through their own branches. The business model of SCARDBs and PCARDBs depends heavily on borrowings; the former borrow from institutions such as NABARD for direct lending as well as lending through PCARDBs. The financial health of PCARDBs is, however, more fragile than SCARDBs, given the high share of accumulated losses on their balance sheets. A2. This revolutionary initiative not only facilitates the identification of active cooperative societies, but also assists the Government in the formulation of policies to strengthen the cooperative sector to elevate the standard of living for the underprivileged and marginalized sections of society. 2.2 Need for Database Despite India being home to almost 25% of total cooperative societies in the world and with history of cooperative movement in India dating back to more than a century, there was no comprehensive, authentic and updated data repository in the country about cooperatives, their activities, their members, their financial details etc. The availability of organized database of the cooperatives, can help in formulating programs and schemes, mentioning the exact number of beneficiaries. The Ministry of Cooperation was constituted on 6th July, 2021 with a mandate, inter alia to strengthen cooperative movement in the country and deepening its reach up to grassroots; and creation of appropriate policy, legal and institutional framework to help cooperatives realize their potential. Profile C ooperative movement started in 1904 in the state and country with the objective to provide short-term crop loan to common people especially rural farmers for their economic development. Later, other program such as fertilizers, distribution of seeds, process units/cold storage, distribution of consumer goods, long-term loans, labour organization, dairy development, sugar cane industry, housing, handloom development etc. were also started through cooperative societies. Due to expansion of cooperative movement/programs, the power of Registrar, Cooperative Societies has been delegated to the officers of 9 other departments, viz., Sugarcane, Industry, Khadi and Village Industry, Housing, Milk, Handloom, Fishery, Silk and Horticulture. The cooperative societies are managed by representatives elected in democratic manner which promote people’s participation. Uttar Pradesh Cooperative and Village Development Bank provides long-term loans for agriculture and non-agriculture sector through its branches. Urban Cooperative Banks of the State provide consumer loan, housing loan, vehicle loan and business loan in their area of operation. To save the farmers from the exploitation of middleman, wheat and paddy are purchased by the cooperative societies under price support program of state government. Additional storage capacity is being created to enhance the present storage capacity of cooperative societies. A total of 43,362 cooperative societies are registered in 75 districts of Uttar Pradesh with membership of 1,84,64,158 members. Lucknow, Agra and Prayagraj districts have the highest number of societies viz. 1543, 1490 and 1468 respectively. Dairy sector is the largest sector constituting of 41.17% (17,852) cooperatives. It is followed by PACS which constitute 17.39% (7541) cooperatives. Notably, 50.84% (93,87,212) of the total members are engaged in PACS. 77.51% (33,609) of the societies are working in rural areas. Though PACS constitute 17.39% of the cooperatives, their Gram Panchayat coverage is extensive (96.16%). Dairy cooperatives cover 27.01% of the Gram Panchayats. Majority of the PACS 5414 are affiliated with Federations/ Unions. Uttar Pradesh

Profile C ooperatives in Jharkhand are dedicated to fostering comprehensive economic and social development for small and marginal farmers, artisans, and various societies. Their operations aim to uplift the people of the state, with a particular focus on the tribal community. Recognizing agriculture as the lifeline of the state’s residents, cooperatives have played a pivotal role in this endeavour. The Cooperative Department’s overarching objective is to provide short and medium-term production credit through a network of LAMPS (Large Area Multipurpose Societies) and PACS (Primary Agriculture Credit Societies), facilitated by the Jharkhand State Cooperative Bank Ltd. Ranchi, District Central Co-operative Bank Ltd. Dhanbad, and Vyapar Mandal Sahyog Samities etc. Presently Jharkhand has 11,409 cooperative societies, out of which 7,267 are a functional, 3,952 are non-functional, and 190 are under liquidation. Of these, 9,773 societies are located in the rural sector, while 1,636 operate in the urban sector, collectively providing membership to 20,92,988 individuals. In operational sectors, Primary Agriculture Credit Societies (PACS) lead with 4,411societies and 14,38,615 members. PACS in the state function as multiservice centres, serving as one-stop shops for farmers by offering storage, procurement, and marketing facilities. The Women’s Welfare Cooperative Society, covering 11.6% of cooperatives, boasts 1,06,061 memberships. Notably, when examining the coverage of Gram Panchayats (GPs) on the National Cooperatives Database (NCD) portal, PACS have a remarkable 98.3% coverage, with Giridih district having the highest number of GPs with PACS. The audit of 924 PACS reveals that 75.9% are affiliated with banks. Jharkhand

मतिान करने की अनुमजत िी िाएगी । ऐसी ििा में भुगतान की गई आपजत्त फीस िब् त कर ली िाएगी । (10) मतिान के अंत में ररटर्नंग अजधकारी एकजत्रत आपजत्त फीस, आपजत्त करने वाले ्‍ यजियों को वापस की गई फीस और िब् त की गई फीस का जहसाब तैयार करेगा और साथ में प्रत् येक मामले में संजिप् त िांच के पश् चातम उसके द्वारा जलए गए जनणायों का संजिप् त सार सोसाइटी को िेगा । (11) यदि मतिान के दकसी चरण में, िंगा या हंगामा द्वारा कायावाही अवरुद्ध या बाजधत होती है या यदि ऐसे जनवााचन में दकसी पयााप् त कारणों से मतिान कराना संभव नहीं है तो ररटर्नंग अजधकारी को मतिान रे करने के ऐसे कारणों को अजभलेजखत करने के पश् चातम, मतिान रे करने की िजि होगी । (12) मतिान के जलए जनयत समय के पश् चातम दकसी मतिाता को मतिान करने की अनुमजत नहीं िी िाएगी । परंतु दक यदि कोई मतिाता, मतिान के समय की समाजप्त के पूवा पररसर में प्रवेि कर चुका हो तो उसे मतपत्र िारी कर मतिान करने की अनुमजत िी िाएगी । (13) मतिान की समाजप्त के ीक पश् चातम मतगणना आरंभ की िाएगी और यदि ररटर्नंग अजधकारी के जनयंत्रण से परे यदि मतों की गणना तुरंत संभव नहीं है तो मतपेटी को ररटर्नंग अजधकारी और जनवााचन में खड़े अभ् यर्थायों या उनके एिेंटों के मुहरों से मुहरबंि कर दिया िाएगा, और यदि यह उनकी इच् छा हो तो मतपेरटयां सोसाइटी की सुरजित अजभरिा में िमा कर िी िाएगी और ऐसी जस्ट्थजत में ररटर्नंग अजधकारी अगले दिन आरंभ होने वाली मतगणना का स्ट् थान और समय की घोिणा करेगा और अभ् यथी और उसके अजभकतााओं को जलजखत में भी सूजचत करेगा और मतगणना अगले दिन ररटर्नंग अजधकारी द्वारा या उसके पयावेिण में की िाएगी और प्रत् येक अभ् यथी और उनके प्राजधकृत अजभकताा को मतगणना के समय उपजस्ट्थत रहने का अजधकार होगा तथा दकसी अभ् यथी या उसके अजभकताा के मतगणना में अनुपजस्ट्थत रहने से ररटर्नंग अजधकारी द्वारा मतगणना या पररणाम की घोिणा जनष् प्रभावी नहीं होगी । (14) ररटर्नंग अजधकारी द्वारा मतगणना की समाजप्त के पश् चातम, वह मतिान के पररणाम की एक जववरणी तैयार करेगा और प्राजधकरण के पूवाानुमोिन से तुरंत पररणाम घोजित करेगा ।

ररटर्नंग अजधकारी, उसके द्वारा प्राप् त नामांकनों की सूची तैयार कर सोसाइटी की नोरटस बोडा में प्रिर्िात करेगा और ऐसा कोई नामांकन प्रूपप िो उसकी प्राजप्त के जलए जनयत तारीख और समय पर या उससे पहले प्राप् त नहीं होता है, को रे कर दिया िाएगा । (5) बोडा के ररक्ट् त स्ट् थान को भरने के जलए जनवााचन में ऐसे दकसी ्‍ यजि को अभ् यथी के ूपप में नामांदकत नहीं दकया िाएगा यदि वह - (क) मतिान के जलए अपात्र हो; (ख) अर्हात न हो या अजधजनयम या इन जनयमों के उपबंधों के अधीन दकसी बहुराज् य सहकारी सोसाइटी के सिस्ट् य के ूपप में या बोडा के सिस्ट् य के ूपप में अयोग् य हराया गया हो; और (ग) बोडा के सिस्ट् य के ूप प में जनवााचन हेतु सोसाइटी की उपजवजधयों में जवजनर्िाष् ट आवश् यक अहाताएं नहीं रखता हो । 19ट. अजधजनयम की धारा 43 और 44 का अनुपालन - बोडा के सिस्ट् य, और पिाजधकाररयों के जनवााचन के जलए अभ् यर्थायों की पात्रता अजधजनयम की धारा 43 और 44 में जनजहत उपबंधों के अध् याधीन होंगी । 19 . नामांकन पत्र की छानबीन - (1) नामांकन पत्र की छानबीन के जलए जनयत दिन को – (क) ररटर्नंग अजधकारी जनर्िाष् ट समय पर नामांकन पत्र की छानबीन का काया करेगा और अभ् यथी या प्रत् येक अभ् यथी का प्रस्ट् तावक या अनुसमथाक, नामांकन पत्र की िांच के समय उस स्ट् थान पर उपजस्ट्थत रह सकता है ।

Primary Agricultural Credit Societies (PACS) are village- or panchayat-level cooperative societies that form the lowest tier of the Short-Term Cooperative Credit Structure. PACS deal directly with rural and agricultural borrowers. They provide loans, collect repayment of loans, and may undertake distribution and marketing functions. PACS are an important link between farmers and the higher levels of the cooperative credit system, including District Central Cooperative Banks (DCCBs), State Cooperative Banks (StCBs), and NABARD. --- ## Why are PACS Important? PACS help connect farmers and rural communities with: * Agricultural credit * Farm inputs * Agricultural services * Storage facilities * Markets and distribution * Other cooperative and government-supported services The Ministry of Cooperation describes PACS as the grassroots base of the cooperative credit structure. PACS can help bring farmers closer to credit, agricultural inputs, markets and value addition. --- ## What Services Can PACS Provide? Traditional PACS activities include: * Short-term agricultural credit * Medium-term credit * Distribution of seeds * Distribution of fertilizers * Distribution of pesticides * Storage-related services * Agricultural input services * Marketing and distribution functions * Loan repayment and related credit services Under the Model Bye-laws and diversification initiatives, PACS can also undertake multiple activities beyond traditional credit. These may include: * Dairy activities * Fisheries activities * Floriculture * Food-grain procurement * Warehousing and storage * Fair Price Shops * LPG/CNG/Petrol/Diesel distributorship * Common Service Centre (CSC) services * Business Correspondent or banking-related activities * Insurance-related services * Custom Hiring Centres * Other permitted business activities The exact activities available at an individual PACS depend on its applicable State Cooperative Societies Act, bye-laws, permissions and local implementation. --- ## What Types of Loans Does PACS Provide? PACS traditionally provide: * Short-term agricultural credit * Medium-term agricultural credit The Model Bye-laws and computerization framework also cover financial services involving short-, medium- and long-term loans. However, the exact loan products, limits, interest rates, repayment periods and eligibility conditions depend on the applicable cooperative rules, State provisions and the individual PACS or financing structure. 36 National Cooperative Database 2023 : A Report P rimary Agriculture Credit Societies (PACS) constitute the lowest tier of the Short-Term Cooperative Credit Structure (STCCS) in the country, primarily providing short-term and medium-term credit facility and other input services, like seed, fertilizer, pesticide distribution, etc. to member farmers. PACS are refinanced by NABARD through District Central Cooperative Banks (DCCBs) and State Cooperative Banks (StCBs). Being the grassroots level cooperative institutions, PACS play a crucial role in sustaining the rural economy of the country by purveying institutional credit to small and marginal farmers. PACS are governed by the Cooperative Acts of their respective states and guided by State Bye-laws. They engage directly with rural (agricultural) borrowers, extending loans, overseeing loan repayments, and managing marketing and distribution functions. Notably, the National Cooperative Database (NCD) portal records the presence of 1,03,304 PACS in the country, with around 95% (i.e., 98,486) of them are being functional in rural areas. Significantly, the growth of PACS has been substantial, expanding from approximately 2,982 PACS in 1900-1923 to 14,391 PACS in 2011-2023. Maharashtra has the highest number of PACS (21,059) followed by Gujarat (10,266) and Bihar (8,476). Kerala boasts the highest number of members (2,56,28,261), trailed by Bihar (1,36,29,113) and Tamil Nadu (1,33,39,395). Around 78% PACS (78,489) are affiliated with Federations/ Unions. Out of total 2,69,503 gram panchayats, around 89% (i.e., 2,41,075) panchayats are covered under PACS. Importantly, strengthening PACS involves enhancing their capacity and effectiveness to provide a spectrum of services to farmers and rural communities beyond credit and financial services. Governments and stakeholders aim to uplift rural communities, improve the overall state of agriculture, and foster inclusive economic growth by reinforcing PACS. These efforts will contribute towards reducing poverty, ensuring food security, and promoting sustainable development in agrarian economies. A1. top3.text: 3 PACS Computerisation Project - Guidelines 1 Introduction The Primary Agriculture Credit Societies (PACS) form the vital third tier in the three- tier structure of the Short Term Cooperative Credit Structure (STCCS). The other two tiers are comprised of District Central Cooperative Bank (DCCBs) (2nd tier) and State Cooperative Bank (StCBs) (1st tier). National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development (NABARD), has earlier taken the initiative to bring most of the StCBs and DCCBs on Core Banking Solutions (CBS) platform which has enabled them to give modern-day technology-based banking facilities to their clients. However, the PACS have so far been largely out of the ambit of the technology support. PACS are owned by farmers, rural artisans etc. and aim at promoting thrift and mutual help among the members; cater to their credit requirements and provide credit-linked services like input supply, storage and marketing of agricultural produce etc. DCCBs provide direct linkages to the PACS through direct financing. The StCBs are primarily responsible for control and coordination of the finances of DCCBs. The large out-reach of PACS to the Small and Marginal Farmers (SMFs) make them a systemically important class of agricultural credit purveying institutions. Further, there is a felt need to develop cooperatives as vibrant business enterprises by enabling them to provide multiple services to their members with support of technology in order to fulfil members’ requirements. Keeping in view the above and to make PACS self-reliant in tune with ‘Atmanirbhar Bharat Abhiyaan’, the Government of India (GoI) has, on 29th June 2022 approved the Centrally Sponsored Project for Computerisation of Primary Agricultural Credit Societies for a period of five years from 2022-23 to 2026-27. 2 Aims & Objectives of the Project The aims and objectives of the project inter alia include the following: a. 49 Sector-wise Cooperatives L ong-term rural credit cooperatives were established for providing funds for investment in agriculture – including land development, farm mechanisation and minor irrigation - rural industries and housing. This structure consists of 14 State Cooperative Agriculture and Rural Development Banks (SCARDBs) operating at the state level and 533 Primary Cooperative Agriculture and Rural Development Banks (PCARDBs) operating at the district/ block level. The structure of long-term rural credit cooperatives differs across states. States like Jammu and Kashmir, Tripura, Uttar Pradesh, Gujarat and Puducherry follow a unitary structure i.e., SCARDBs operate through their own branches with no separate PCARDBs. On the other hand, states like Haryana, Punjab, Rajasthan, Karnataka, Kerala, and Tamil Nadu follow a federal structure wherein SCARDBs lend through PCARDBs. In two states viz., Himachal Pradesh and West Bengal, SCARDBs operate through PCARDBs as well as through their own branches. The business model of SCARDBs and PCARDBs depends heavily on borrowings; the former borrow from institutions such as NABARD for direct lending as well as lending through PCARDBs. The financial health of PCARDBs is, however, more fragile than SCARDBs, given the high share of accumulated losses on their balance sheets. A2. Cooperative banks are basically cooperative societies which are registered under the Cooperative Societies Act of the State concerned or under the Multi-State Cooperative Societies (Amendment) Act, 2023. While cooperative societies functioning within a single state are governed by Cooperative Societies Act of their respective state, cooperative societies functioning in more than one State/ UT are governed by Multi-State Cooperative Societies (Amendment) Act, 2023 under the purview of Government of India. When cooperative societies carry on the business of banking, they come under the regulatory purview of RBI and they are licensed under the provisions of the Banking Regulation Act. The cooperative banking structure in India was developed to complement and supplement the commercial banking structure, with a specific focus on serving the requirements of marginalised borrowers and meeting the development needs of rural as well as urban areas. Urban Cooperative Banks (UCBs) are classified as scheduled and non-scheduled, based on their inclusion or otherwise in the second schedule of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934, and their geographical outreach (single-state or multi-state). Rural cooperatives are segregated by their lending activity, i.e., into short-term vis-à-vis long-term lending. Rural credit short-term credits are channelled through StCB, DCCBs and PACS. Primary Agricultural Credit Societies (PACS) are village- or panchayat-level cooperative societies that form the lowest tier of the Short-Term Cooperative Credit Structure. PACS deal directly with rural and agricultural borrowers. They provide loans, collect repayment of loans, and may undertake distribution and marketing functions. PACS are an important link between farmers and the higher levels of the cooperative credit system, including District Central Cooperative Banks (DCCBs), State Cooperative Banks (StCBs), and NABARD. --- ## Why are PACS Important? PACS help connect farmers and rural communities with: * Agricultural credit * Farm inputs * Agricultural services * Storage facilities * Markets and distribution * Other cooperative and government-supported services The Ministry of Cooperation describes PACS as the grassroots base of the cooperative credit structure. PACS can help bring farmers closer to credit, agricultural inputs, markets and value addition. --- ## What Services Can PACS Provide? Traditional PACS activities include: * Short-term agricultural credit * Medium-term credit * Distribution of seeds * Distribution of fertilizers * Distribution of pesticides * Storage-related services * Agricultural input services * Marketing and distribution functions * Loan repayment and related credit services Under the Model Bye-laws and diversification initiatives, PACS can also undertake multiple activities beyond traditional credit. These may include: * Dairy activities * Fisheries activities * Floriculture * Food-grain procurement * Warehousing and storage * Fair Price Shops * LPG/CNG/Petrol/Diesel distributorship * Common Service Centre (CSC) services * Business Correspondent or banking-related activities * Insurance-related services * Custom Hiring Centres * Other permitted business activities The exact activities available at an individual PACS depend on its applicable State Cooperative Societies Act, bye-laws, permissions and local implementation. --- ## What Types of Loans Does PACS Provide? PACS traditionally provide: * Short-term agricultural credit * Medium-term agricultural credit The Model Bye-laws and computerization framework also cover financial services involving short-, medium- and long-term loans. However, the exact loan products, limits, interest rates, repayment periods and eligibility conditions depend on the applicable cooperative rules, State provisions and the individual PACS or financing structure. 36 National Cooperative Database 2023 : A Report P rimary Agriculture Credit Societies (PACS) constitute the lowest tier of the Short-Term Cooperative Credit Structure (STCCS) in the country, primarily providing short-term and medium-term credit facility and other input services, like seed, fertilizer, pesticide distribution, etc. to member farmers. PACS are refinanced by NABARD through District Central Cooperative Banks (DCCBs) and State Cooperative Banks (StCBs). Being the grassroots level cooperative institutions, PACS play a crucial role in sustaining the rural economy of the country by purveying institutional credit to small and marginal farmers. PACS are governed by the Cooperative Acts of their respective states and guided by State Bye-laws. They engage directly with rural (agricultural) borrowers, extending loans, overseeing loan repayments, and managing marketing and distribution functions. Notably, the National Cooperative Database (NCD) portal records the presence of 1,03,304 PACS in the country, with around 95% (i.e., 98,486) of them are being functional in rural areas. Significantly, the growth of PACS has been substantial, expanding from approximately 2,982 PACS in 1900-1923 to 14,391 PACS in 2011-2023. Maharashtra has the highest number of PACS (21,059) followed by Gujarat (10,266) and Bihar (8,476). Kerala boasts the highest number of members (2,56,28,261), trailed by Bihar (1,36,29,113) and Tamil Nadu (1,33,39,395). Around 78% PACS (78,489) are affiliated with Federations/ Unions. Out of total 2,69,503 gram panchayats, around 89% (i.e., 2,41,075) panchayats are covered under PACS. Importantly, strengthening PACS involves enhancing their capacity and effectiveness to provide a spectrum of services to farmers and rural communities beyond credit and financial services. Governments and stakeholders aim to uplift rural communities, improve the overall state of agriculture, and foster inclusive economic growth by reinforcing PACS. These efforts will contribute towards reducing poverty, ensuring food security, and promoting sustainable development in agrarian economies. A1. top3.text: 3 PACS Computerisation Project - Guidelines 1 Introduction The Primary Agriculture Credit Societies (PACS) form the vital third tier in the three- tier structure of the Short Term Cooperative Credit Structure (STCCS). The other two tiers are comprised of District Central Cooperative Bank (DCCBs) (2nd tier) and State Cooperative Bank (StCBs) (1st tier). National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development (NABARD), has earlier taken the initiative to bring most of the StCBs and DCCBs on Core Banking Solutions (CBS) platform which has enabled them to give modern-day technology-based banking facilities to their clients. However, the PACS have so far been largely out of the ambit of the technology support. PACS are owned by farmers, rural artisans etc. and aim at promoting thrift and mutual help among the members; cater to their credit requirements and provide credit-linked services like input supply, storage and marketing of agricultural produce etc. DCCBs provide direct linkages to the PACS through direct financing. The StCBs are primarily responsible for control and coordination of the finances of DCCBs. The large out-reach of PACS to the Small and Marginal Farmers (SMFs) make them a systemically important class of agricultural credit purveying institutions. Further, there is a felt need to develop cooperatives as vibrant business enterprises by enabling them to provide multiple services to their members with support of technology in order to fulfil members’ requirements. The structure of long-term rural credit cooperatives differs across states. States like Jammu and Kashmir, Tripura, Uttar Pradesh, Gujarat and Puducherry follow a unitary structure i.e., SCARDBs operate through their own branches with no separate PCARDBs. On the other hand, states like Haryana, Punjab, Rajasthan, Karnataka, Kerala, and Tamil Nadu follow a federal structure wherein SCARDBs lend through PCARDBs. In two states viz., Himachal Pradesh and West Bengal, SCARDBs operate through PCARDBs as well as through their own branches. The business model of SCARDBs and PCARDBs depends heavily on borrowings; the former borrow from institutions such as NABARD for direct lending as well as lending through PCARDBs.
